entries.title: Appeals Court Questions Trump Administration’s Bid to Block 20,000 California Ballots
entries.summary: The DOJ is suing the state in an effort to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots the Trump administration believes California sent to noncitizens.
entries.content:
The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals appeared skeptical of the Justice Department’s effort to compel California to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots the Trump administration suspects may have been sent to noncitizens.

Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly faced several questions from a three-judge panel of the appellate court about the timing of the Justice Department’s lawsuit, which was filed Oct. 15, seeking to force the state to check its voter list against one the federal government created of suspected noncitizens. A sticking point came Sunday from whether a third-party vendor was involved in that list.

“If you take a step back, you are not able to explain who these third parties are that form some part in the chain of analysis over this list,” U.S. Circuit Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, a Biden appointee, said to Donnelly “Your claims very much depend on the reliability of that list.”

The rare Sunday hearing before the appellate court came after the Justice Department demanded a lower court rule by Oct. 22.

Donnelly pushed back when U.S. Circuit Judge Mark J. Bennett, a Trump appointee, asked if the Justice Department could have filed its lawsuit against California earlier because Donnelly “certainly knew that there was in your mind a problem well before that.”

“We could have filed a complaint, but we wanted to file the complaint that we filed,” Donnelly said, adding that the Trump administration had not fully processed the list of 20,000 voters that it delivered to California election officials before the date it filed the lawsuit.

California deputy attorney general, Samuel Siegel, said that his state has attestation rules requiring voters to certify that they are U.S. citizens and meet the other eligibility standards before casting their ballots.

“The executive branch may not like the way that California administers its elections, but nothing in the Constitution, the U.S. Code, or any other source of law entitles it to the extraordinary remedy that it's seeking,” Siegel told the court.

Bennett appeared to agree and said that he has “a problem with the relief that's being sought” by the administration because both “Congress and the California legislature have said noncitizens can't vote.”

Bennett added that he sees the Justice Department’s lawsuit as effectively telling California “we don't like the way you're sorting citizens from noncitizens” and noted that he does does not believe the federal law prohibiting noncitizens from voting allows the Trump administration to tell “California how to do the sorting.”

The appellate court did not immediately issue a ruling.

The hearing Sunday comes nine days before the midterms and centers on the 20,000 ballots that Homeland Security Investigations and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services have identified as potential noncitizens on the California voter rolls.

The Justice Department sent California election officials a letter and a password-protected thumb drive on Oct. 13 with a 48-hour countdown to cross-reference the list of names against state voter lists. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, said the DOJ identified voters it “believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot.”

California is one of six states that automatically sends out a mail-in ballot to every registered voter before an election, and the state started sending out ballots on Oct. 5.

On Oct. 15, the Justice Department sued the state of California and election officials Weber and Dean Logan, the registrar for Los Angeles County. The department pushed for an expedited ruling, and U.S. District Judge David O. Carter scheduled a hearing for Oct. 27.

The Justice Department wanted a decision sooner, and petitioned the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals for it to step in.

entries.title: Hegseth’s Military Promotion Blocks Could Face a Congressional Reckoning
entries.summary: As House Democrats weigh oversight priorities, the incoming Congressional Black Caucus chair wants investigating the treatment of Black and female officers to top the list.
entries.content:
The incoming chair of the Congressional Black Caucus says Democrats could subpoena Pentagon officials to investigate allegations of racial and gender discrimination in military promotions under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth if they regain control of the House in November.

The warning from Rep. Troy Carter (D-Louisiana) puts the considerable political weight of the influential caucus behind calls for an aggressive investigation as Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee prepare their potential oversight agenda.

Hegseth’s personnel decisions are among the Democratic priorities, but they are just part of a crowded oversight agenda, and lawmakers have yet to decide how any probe would proceed. Carter’s push could help determine how prominently the issue figures into those plans.

“We will have subpoena power, and he can test it if he wants to,” Carter said of Hegseth. “This is a new and improved Democratic Party, and we enforce the rules. The time to play nice is far spent.”

“You cannot just summarily remove people who've done nothing wrong, who have committed to America and our safety, and then summarily remove them because you don't like their gender, or you don't like the color of their skin,” Carter said.

At the center of the dispute is Hegseth’s reported removal of officers — a disproportionate number of whom were women and people of color — from promotion lists assembled through the military’s established selection process. The decisions have raised concerns among lawmakers and military advocates that political or ideological considerations are displacing professional qualifications in determining who advances to the military’s highest ranks.

Hegseth removed at least 45 senior officers from promotion lists across the armed services, more than half of whom were women or Black officers, according to an investigation The New York Times published in August. Hegseth’s aides also reportedly had established a vetting process that examined officers’ public statements, photographs, speeches and past participation in diversity initiatives.

Just eight of the 201 officers nominated for promotion to general or admiral during the first seven months of 2026 were women — the lowest share in at least 25 years.

The promotion decisions are part of a broader shake-up of military personnel policies and senior military firings under President Donald Trump. He fired Gen. CQ Brown, the second Black chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; Adm. Lisa Franchetti, the first woman to serve as chief of naval operations; and Adm. Linda Fagan, the first woman to lead a branch of the armed forces, as commandant of the Coast Guard.

The Trump administration has also restored Confederate-associated names to military installations, dismantled diversity-related programs, and advocates say the Pentagon’s ongoing study of women serving in combat roles could lead to their participation being restricted.

Hegseth has defended his broader personnel changes as necessary to restore meritocracy and military readiness, arguing that diversity initiatives elevated race and gender over qualifications.

The Pentagon, in response to questions, rejected allegations that race or gender played a role in Hegseth’s promotion decisions, accusing critics of prioritizing identity over qualifications.

“As we’ve said before, military promotions are given to those who have earned them,” chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement. “The Department will never consider the color of a service member’s skin or their gender as a factor in promotions. Under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth, meritocracy reigns supreme at the War Department.”

The promotion decisions are already taking a toll on troop morale, retention and confidence in the military’s advancement system, according to advocates for service members and veterans. They warn that officers may reconsider their military futures if they believe qualifications no longer dictate their prospects for promotion.

The blocked promotions have been “absolutely demoralizing,” said Kyle Bibby, a former Marine infantry captain and co-founder of the Black Veterans Project.

“The message is clear on who they believe should be allowed to serve,” he said. “They want people in those groups to know that they're not desired and to make them feel uncomfortable about their service.”

Carter said that if Democrats control the House, the Congressional Black Caucus would use “every tool in our tool shed to bring about awareness and justice,” pressing for hearings, investigations and legislation to hold Pentagon leaders accountable.

He said he has discussed the administration’s actions with other Democrats, including lawmakers involved in national security and oversight. Carter said that Rep. Adam Smith (D-Washington), the House Armed Services Committee’s top Democrat, is among those taking the issue seriously.

Pressure from Carter’s 62-member caucus could elevate the issue as lawmakers juggle competing priorities. Its members include high-ranking members of the House and Senate, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.

“Their collective voice represents millions of individuals across the country, and after Nov. 3, if Democrats win, you’ll have more African-Americans in positions of leadership than we’ve ever had, so it carries the weight of a metric ton,” said Bakari Sellers, a Democratic commentator and former South Carolina lawmaker.

Carter’s remarks came weeks after the Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee met to grapple with a crowded oversight agenda that could include investigations into the Iran war, Pentagon contracting, military strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats and more.

According to a HASC staffer who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, lawmakers are still working out how to coordinate investigations with the House Oversight and Judiciary committees and when to dust off its seldom-used subpoena power, which Smith has publicly said he would be willing to invoke.

Smith has already identified Hegseth’s personnel decisions as an oversight priority, citing concerns about their impact on military recruitment and readiness — and discussed the issue with Congressional Black Caucus leadership, the staffer said. But it remains undecided whether there would be a formal investigation, according to the staffer. Also uncertain is which committee would take the lead and whether subpoenas would be involved.

Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colorado), an Army veteran and member of the House Armed Services Committee, said that panel Democrats have already been documenting the decisions and discussing potential investigation targets.

“We are being very intentional, very strategic, keeping close notes on what’s happening,” Crow said.

“I'm deeply concerned about the purges of the senior ranks, the politicization of what should be a merit-based promotion system,” Crow said, calling for “a very vigorous oversight and investigation of this to try to unravel what's been happening and to seek accountability.”

Rep. Gil Cisneros (D-California), who served as the Pentagon’s undersecretary for personnel and readiness during the Biden administration, said previous defense secretaries traditionally relied on the military services’ recommendations for one- and two-star promotions, but they typically took a more active role in selecting the most senior commanders.

Officers could be removed from promotion lists, he said, but usually because of misconduct allegations. Cisneros described Hegseth’s removal of officers without publicly explaining the decisions as a sharp departure, which he called “definitely political interference.”

“The [congressional] investigation should show that what’s going on right now is not normal,” Cisneros said.

Legislation introduced this month by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) and Reps. Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pennsylvania) and Marilyn Strickland (D-Washington) would restrict the grounds for removing officers from promotion lists, require documentation and establish a formal review process.

But that bill, the Military Officer Promotion Integrity Act, would apply to future decisions and would not affect promotions that were already blocked.

The consequences of missing a promotion extend well beyond losing a higher rank. Officers can lose access to command assignments, training and other opportunities essential to advancing their careers.

“It's an up-or-out organization, so you can't really get back what you've lost,” said Sue Fulton, the executive director of the Women in the Service Coalition, Inc.

Advocacy organizations say the uncertainty is already affecting how service members think about their futures — and that they are too afraid of reprisals to speak out.

“Our active duty members are too terrified, frankly, to come forward when they don't necessarily know if they're going to be protected,” said Rita Graham, policy director of the Service Women’s Action Network.

The National Women’s Law Center is also pressing for accountability, while its affiliated advocacy arm has endorsed Blumenthal’s legislation.

Adrienne DerVartanian, senior counsel for education and workplace justice at the organization, argued that removing qualified officers for political or ideological reasons is “incredibly harmful to morale” and makes the military less effective.

“I think we’re all safer,” she said, “when we focus on qualifications and not stereotypes.”

entries.title: Mystics’ Shakira Austin Named to All-WNBA Second Team
entries.summary: The veteran center is the franchise’s first player since 2021 to earn all-league honors.
entries.content:
Mystics center Shakira Austin continues to rack up honors after a career season.

On Saturday, Austin was named to the All-WNBA second team after a season in which she averaged 17 points and 9.5 rebounds. Austin, a Fredericksburg, Virginia, native, shot 48% from the field and led the team in total points, rebounds and blocks. She was also named to the WNBA’s All-Defensive first team on Oct. 15.

She finished fourth in voting for Defensive Player of the Year (won by Angel Reese) and ninth in MVP voting. Aces star A’ja Wilson was named MVP for a record fifth time and became the first player to win the honor in three consecutive seasons.

Austin, 26, is the seventh player in Mystics franchise history to be named to an all-league team and the first since Tina Charles in 2021. This season, she became the first Washington player and just the seventh player in WNBA history to post a 25-game streak of at least 10 points and five or more rebounds.

The Mystics selected Austin third overall out of Mississippi in 2022. Austin, who graduated from Riverdale Baptist School in Maryland, led Washington to its best season in years. The team finished the regular season with a 28–16 record and earned the fifth seed in the WNBA playoffs before losing to the Atlanta Dream in the first round. It was the organization’s first postseason berth since 2023 and highest regular season win total since 2019.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Launches ‘The Stakeout’ Newsletter
entries.summary: The newsletter will be helmed by Sun reporters Igor Bobic and Oriana González.
entries.content:
The Washington Sun is launching “The Stakeout,” a newsletter you’ll need and want to read about what’s really going on in the halls of Congress. Led by Sun congressional reporters Igor Bobic and Oriana González, The Stakeout will deliver scoops, behind-the scenes details on the news of the day and impactful reporting on the lives of those who spend their days in the U.S. Capitol. The Stakeout will feature extensive reporting from The Sun’s Hill team: Kadia Goba, Reese Gorman, Avani Kalra, Paul Kane, Stephen Neukam and Al Weaver.

Bobic and González have spent years covering the Capitol and the people who work there — from lawmakers to the thousands of people who make the place run.

“The world’s greatest deliberative body? Well, it depends on the day,” said Bobic. “But we’re excited to cover and obsess over this complex cast of characters of the Capitol in a fun and informative way.”

"Before you say, 'Oh no, not another newsletter,' let me tell you that you're going to want to read this one," said González. “Come for the scoops, stay because you're reading something you actually enjoy."

The first edition will premier on Monday, Nov. 9. Join The Stakeout by signing up here.

About The Washington Sun


We launched in 2024 as NOTUS, a news site focused on national politics and policy. But as we watched others pull back on Washington coverage, we knew our hometown deserved better. So we invested, more than doubling the size of our newsroom in just six months.

Our work puts Washington front and center, and we wanted our name to do the same. So NOTUS — short for News of the United States — is now The Washington Sun.

We cover politics and policy and the people who shape life in Washington — not just at the White House and in Congress, but at the Wilson Building, at Northwest Stadium and in the neighborhoods where we live.

We report for the people who live here, the people who make policy here and the people around the world who care deeply about what happens here. We do it with original reporting, with deep sourcing and with an unwavering commitment to accuracy.

entries.title: Spirit Fall to Kansas City Current, 2-1
entries.summary: Washington couldn't build on Clara Luvunga's early goal in its penultimate regular season game.
entries.content:
Vanessa DiBernardo capped a frantic five-minute stretch with the winning goal in the 17th minute and the Kansas City Current rallied past the Washington Spirit 2-1 on Sunday.

The Current (15-9-5) erased an early deficit with two goals three minutes apart, then held off the visiting Spirit (16-9-4) despite finishing with less than 40% of possession.

Clara Luvunga gave the Spirit the lead in the 12th minute after pouncing on a heavy touch by Kansas City goalkeeper Lorena.

Lo’eau LaBonta pulled Kansas City even, collecting a rebound in the penalty area before firing a shot that deflected off Washington defender Esme Morgan’s leg, sending the ball bouncing past goalkeeper Sandy MacIver.

DiBernardo’s first goal of the season began with pressure from Haley Hopkins, who stripped the ball from MacIver. Hopkins reached the end line and found Croix Bethune, who laid the ball off to DiBernardo for a first-time finish.

Lorena recovered from the early mistake to finish with two crucial saves. MacIver made one.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Raise the Roof
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 26, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

 In today’s newsletter: A roof for Audi Field, Turnstile on the Mall and the Marine Corps Marathon. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 9/10. A little early fog and frost are the only blemishes on an otherwise spectacular fall day. Read the full forecast.

THE LATEST

D.C. United’s new goal is to add 8,000 seats and a roof to Audi Field, but a key part of the deal — public money to help cover the costs — won’t be an easy score.

The D.C. Council is now considering a bill that would contribute $300 million to the project, with the team kicking in $320 million of its own for the expansion of the stadium and construction of more than 400 units of housing on an adjacent parcel of land, The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports.

Team officials and boosters of the proposed deal say it would turn Audi Field into a year-round venue able to host more sporting events, as well as concerts. Along with D.C. United, the venue already hosts the Washington Spirit, Power FC and D.C. Defenders. Proponents say more seats and a roof would both facilitate Major League Soccer’s upcoming schedule change and grow the number of teams able to play there.

Critics say the deal is unnecessary and poorly conceived, even more so in an era where D.C. is facing a slowing economy and leaner budget. The opponents — which include Mayor Muriel Bowser — say Audi Field is only eight years old, was built in part with taxpayer dollars and could cannibalize events at Capital One Arena, which is itself being renovated with $515 million from the city.

The proposed deal faces plenty of obstacles, but a big one is the Spirit. The popular women’s team is currently renegotiating its lease to use Audi Field, and team officials have made little secret of wanting to use the bill as leverage to win things like increased signage, their own locker room and more. “It’s very hard for us to be supportive if you’re not able to bring the Spirit on-side,” said Ward 3 council member Matt Frumin at a hearing last week.

D.C. United has been playing smart politics, though. The team says it has reached an initial agreement with labor unions to ensure that union workers are used on the stadium and housing, nailing down a detail that’s important for many D.C. lawmakers — and is often fought out at the last minute.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Turnstile AP - 26297791251506 (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)
Organizers estimated 60,000 attendees gathered at the Washington Monument on Saturday for Baltimore hardcore band Turnstile’s free show, where donations went toward humanitarian efforts in Palestine, Sudan and Lebanon.

Frontman Brendan Yates asked the crowd to be “loud enough for the White House to hear.”

“Free Palestine. Free Sudan. Free Lebanon. And always, always, keep it moving,” Yates shouted, giving moshers the go-ahead. The Sun’s Paige Huffman witnessed men kicking each other and then hugging gleefully seconds after, Turnstile Orioles shirts, a kid-friendly mosh pit in the back, and mounted Park Police. As of Sunday morning, the show had raised $225,000 for Canadian relief group Human Concern International.

Gretchen Evans was one of thousands who ran the Marine Corps Marathon on Sunday. The 66-year-old’s military career came to an abrupt end in 2006, when a mortar blast in Afghanistan left her with a traumatic brain injury and total hearing loss, but that didn’t take away her love of running. The Sun’s Yasmeen Khan writes that Evans wants to run into her 80s, or, “until the wheels come off.”

The new neighborhood joints: With drinking on the decline, Washingtonians are finding community within cannabis dispensaries, The Sun’s Torrie Herrington reports. Thanks to a 2023 law, D.C. allows licensed medical cannabis retailers to offer on-site consumption areas for patients. The result: an alternative to the traditional bar.

Mind the gap. WMATA is facing a $79 million to $114 million funding gap in its fiscal year 2028 budget, The Sun’s Will Hofmann reports. Despite plans to increase fares by 11.1% in the coming year, higher fuel and paratransit costs have driven up the agency’s expenses, said Chief Financial Officer Dave Rickard during a board meeting. Boosting bus fare compliance — which currently sits at just 37% — could be one way to help close the deficit, Rickard said.

There are more than 1,600 outstanding housing code violations across the buildings Buwa Binitie’s companies own or operate in D.C., including life-threatening issues that have gone unaddressed for years, City Cast D.C. reports.

The landlord made headlines last month after being sued by D.C.’s attorney general for “extreme and pervasive disrepair” at one of his properties, and after his attorney — former AG Karl Racine — crashed a protest to defend him. Tenants living in Binitie’s properties have organized, filing complaints and lawsuits, The 51st reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

The family of a Northern Virginia man who died while in police custody is suing the city of Alexandria and two of its police officers, FOX5 reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Prince George’s County got back the $7.6 million it had awarded to a nonprofit organization after weeks of scrutiny over the circumstances surrounding the award,WUSA 9 reports.

Earlier this month, County Executive Aisha Braveboy requested that the Edward Charles Foundation, a California-based organization that serves as a fiscal sponsor for the nonprofit Community of the Frontline, return all its county-awarded funds after council members Jolene Ivey and Sydney Harrison accused council chair Krystal Oriadha of directing the money to the nonprofit because of personal ties to its leadership.





FROM THE DINING ROOM

Veteran New York restaurateur Danny Meyer (Gramercy Tavern, The Modern, Shake Shack, Union Square Cafe, etc.) is coming to D.C. on Tuesday to talk to Sun food correspondent Tom Sietsema at the Sulgrave Club about his new, best-selling book, “What Could Possibly Go Right?” Ahead of his visit, we asked the visionary behind Union Square Hospitality Group a couple of questions.

What do you wish more diners knew about your industry?

There’s a perceived adversarial relationship between customers and restaurants, especially regarding places that are hard to reserve. People should understand we’re on the same team.

What three New York restaurants that aren’t yours do you tend to frequent?

Borgo, Claud and Elio’s, for Italian, bistro French and Italian, respectively. The first two are headed by USHG alums and the last is where I decided I wanted to be a restaurateur, in 1984.

(His happiest place, though, is home, eating a chicken picked up from Daily Provisions, his all-day cafe and bakery.)





TRIVIA


Which of the following has not been proposed as a major stadium site for D.C. United?

  1. Fort Totten
  2. Westport, Maryland
  3. Poplar Point
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

After Sunday’s XXXXX against the Kansas City Current, the Spirit have just one regular season game remaining. One of the most underrated reasons for Washington’s success this year? Goalkeeper Sandy MacIver. When longtime keeper Aubrey Kingsbury announced she was going on maternity leave this season, MacIver was thrust into a starting role for the first time in three seasons. She has proved more than capable, contributing to a franchise-record 11 shutouts this season. Nicky Wolcott profiles MacIver for The Sun.

Tonight is Game 3 of the World Series, with the Brewers holding a 2-0 lead over the Rays. The Sun’s Thomas Boswell writes that this year’s series should be called “the Brainiac Classic,” as Tampa Bay and Milwaukee are two of the league’s most analytics-minded teams. Although they represent small markets, both franchises have spent heavily on baseball science and that investment has paid off.

What to Watch Today

NBA: Wizards at Hornets, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

NFL: Cowboys at Eagles, 8:15 p.m. (ESPN)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

entries.title: Morning Sun: Quiet Part, Loudly
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Latest from across the map. Alaska may actually just have a lot of people named Dan Sullivan. More on Trump’s potential staff pardons. Jamie Raskin has a new Epstein report. Live from New Mexico. And: MAGA’s evangelical coalition is fraying. 

THE MAP


Michigan: Trump’s grim closing argument. “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Donald Trump said of Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed at a rally yesterday in Port Huron. He said El-Sayed, if elected, “would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”

Sen. Bernie Sanders responded to Trump at an El-Sayed rally in Grand Rapids: “Mr. President, instead of slandering Abdul and his family, what are you going to do about the health care crisis in America?”

For his part, El-Sayed offered this: “I get that the president of the United States takes personal offense to my first name, he doesn’t mind as much when it’s a shared name from the Saudis who are funding his son-in-law’s private equity.”

Texas: Latino voter watch. Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico appeared at a Voto Latino-sponsored concert headlined by popular norteño band Los Tigres del Norte in Weslaco last night. The Washington Sun’s Daniella Diaz was there, and noted the importance of the location. Trump won this congressional district in 2024, but Democrats are betting the coalition he built in Texas’ border country has crumbled. Voto Latino told Daniella 8,000 people packed it out last night to hear Talarico and a slew of other Democratic candidates.

South Carolina: Stormin’ Normans. Conservative Warren Norman — the son of Republican Rep. Ralph Norman, who lost in the Senate primary to Sen. Darline Graham — said he is “leaning” toward voting for Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews.  Ralph Norman has said he will vote for Graham, but that he won’t do any public appearances with her.

Maine: Trump bails out Susan Collins? The Maine Republican claimed credit for the president loosening some Canadian tariffs, a welcome boost for her campaign against Democrat Troy Jackson.

More: Appeals Court Questions Trump Administration’s Bid to Block 20,000 California Ballots

FROM ALASKA


Are there really too many Dans Sullivan? The president attacked one Alaska Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski, this weekend after she condemned the DOJ effort to preemptively invalidate a possible election loss by the state’s other Republican senator, Dan Sullivan. The whole thing is based on the existence of a Dan J. Sullivan on the Senate ballot, which Trump allies call a dirty trick. Democrats deny any involvement.

Our data reporter Andrew Van Dam looked through a lot of records to find Alaska could be a hotbed for guys named Dan Sullivan. The state is 4th in the nation for number of Dans. It has fewer Sullivans than the national average, but then again Sullivans are several times more likely to be named Dan than the rest of us.

In other Alaska news: Democratic nominee Mary Peltola and her family sustained minor injuries after the vehicle they were traveling in was struck by another vehicle Saturday night.

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


Pardon backlash: “People committing crimes for Trump, or in connection with Trump, take the risk that they will be successfully prosecuted by a future DOJ,” Rep. Ted Lieu (D-California) posted yesterday after The Sun’s Jasmine Wright and Jeff Stein broke the news that the president was considering pardons for lower-level staff. Lieu noted that a blanket pardon has never really been tested by the courts.

Trump doubled down after our reporting, saying it would “be very unfair” for his staff to go through the “corrupt weaponization” that took place under Joe Biden, adding: “I certainly don’t want to see innocent people go through hell and lose all their money.”

New today: House Judiciary Democrats released a report this morning that pulls together years of assault allegations against Trump and his reported connections to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Eight days before the midterms, the report calls for a renewed criminal investigation and further congressional oversight. Much of the information in the report has been out there but it included a new allegation from a Swiss model who claimed the president raped her during a beauty pageant in New York in 1993.

The Sun’s Stephen Neukam reports that the House Oversight Committee, which is leading the congressional Epstein investigation, did not work on the report released from Judiciary Ranking Member Jamie Raskin.

The White House response: “None of these allegations are true. This ‘report’ is nothing more than a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans from the surging Republican momentum driven by President Trump’s historic achievements,” said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis. “The President kicked Jeffrey Epstein out of his club at Mar-a-Lago because he was a creep, and he has been fully exonerated of anything related to Epstein.”

FROM 2028


Meet the New Mexico kingmakers: We were at the inaugural Fourth in the Nation Matanza rally in Albuquerque this weekend — a sort of coming out party for New Mexico’s status as a key player in the Democratic 2028 primary calendar (they’re going fourth, hence the name). The event was hosted by Sen. Ben Ray Luján and featured local pols meeting with two would-be Democratic presidential candidates: Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona (“I’m considering it,” is how he talks about a potential run) and Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland (“I’m kicking the tires”).

We spoke to a lot of local Democratic leaders, and they’re already getting a lot of facetime with these tire-kickers. State House Speaker Javier Martinez told us his phone has been ringing off the hook with calls from people like Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and more. “One of them is actually taking me out for a beer tonight,” he told us Saturday. “That’s the first beer so far.”

More: A Catholic Republican 2028 Nominee Would Make History. Does Anyone Care?





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Evangelicals are not feeling the Trump love this time: “When evangelical voters make up a substantial chunk of that base, and they’re not overly enthusiastic, they’re not excited, they’re frustrated, they don’t necessarily feel like they got what they asked for. That tends to affect enthusiasm and participation,” Cole Muzio, a Republican operative who focuses on Christian outreach, told The Sun. Our Ben T.N. Mause and Andrea Padilla have the story of a major fracture in the coalition that made MAGA happen in the first place: traditional evangelicals and Trump.

entries.title: For This Army Veteran, Running Serves a Higher Purpose
entries.summary: The Marine Corps Marathon holds special meaning for Gretchen Evans, who marked 60 marathons on Sunday.
entries.content:
Gretchen Evans started running long distance in the military. She ran 3 to 5 miles every morning, and occasionally went on lengthier road marches. She had run track in grade school, but the military showed her how much she enjoyed the sport.

“Even though we ran in formation in the military and we're all out there together and we're singing those crazy songs, it always put a smile on my face,” she said. “It always felt like I did something for myself in the morning to start my day. I’m taking care of this, and I can go out and help others.”

Evans, 66, no longer thinks of 5 miles as a long-distance run. On Sunday, she ran in her 60th marathon: the Marine Corps Marathon in D.C.

Evans loves the Marine Corps Marathon for its military ties. The course begins near Arlington National Cemetery and ends at the U.S. Marine Corps War Memorial. Mile 13, which stretches along East Potomac Park, is lined with the photographs of fallen soldiers.

“It’s sacred,” she said.

Evans grew up in Abilene, Texas, a small city in the center of the state. Her father, a World War II veteran, instilled in his children a love of sports and country. Evans played tennis in addition to running track, and her two brothers played football.

Evans’ parents died when she was in middle school. Her oldest brother, then 21, came back to Abilene to help his younger siblings through high school. Evans studied at Texas Tech University for one year, but she struggled to pay for her education on her own.

She joined the military at 19 in order to take advantage of the G.I. Bill. “I thought it was going to be: go four years, get out, finish my education,” she said. She chose to serve in the Army, the same branch as her late father.

Instead, she fell in love with the military. Her service gave her a newfound sense of purpose. “You're part of something that's bigger than yourself,” Evans said. She would go on to serve in the military for 27 years, rising to the position of command sergeant major.

Fourteen years into her military career, Evans ran her first marathon. On the course in Tucson, Arizona, she experienced a communion similar to what she found in military service. “If you want to see the best picture of humanity, go watch a marathon,” she says. “You are trying to do something hard, and you get all these people on the side of the street cheering for people they don't even know. To me, that's a snapshot of what humanity should look like every day.”

Evans’ time in the military came to an abrupt end in Afghanistan in 2006, when a mortar blast caused a traumatic brain injury and total hearing loss. She checked into the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda where she spent months recovering and learning how to live as a deaf person.

Three months into her stay, Evans ran her first mile around the Walter Reed campus, weeping. “I thought ‘I can still do this,’” she said.

In the years since, running has become indispensable to her healing process.

“The rocket blast took my hearing. The rocket blast certainly changed the dynamics of the way my brain works. It rearranged my face a little bit,” she said. “But what I didn't want the rocket blast to take was the things that I love, and running was one of those.”

As Evans reintegrated into civilian life, she sought out a new organizing mission for herself. “I wanted that feeling of doing something that was bigger than me, something that was helping people, something that made a difference in my world,” she said.

She formed Team Unbroken, a running team composed of disabled athletes. “I wanted to take my passion for running and have other people experience how healing it could be,” she said.

Team Unbroken includes both veteran and civilian athletes. Veterans, she said, have a tendency to self-isolate. Leading Team Unbroken became a way for Evans to help other veterans adapt to the civilian world. “I purposely put civilians on my team so that we would learn about each other,” she said. “The best way to learn about somebody is to do something really hard with them, right?”

Coming off the Marine Corps Marathon, Evans’ only goal is to keep going.

“I want to be running in my 80s,” she said. “I want to enjoy running until the wheels come off.”

entries.title: Inside the Trump Administration's Dismantling of a Health Care Research Office
entries.summary: The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality has few remaining grant officers and has redirected millions in taxpayer dollars without telling Congress.
entries.content:
Researchers received letters last spring about their federal grant applications from a Department of Health and Human Services employee who hadn’t worked for the government in months.

Anna Caponiti, a former HHS grant specialist, had been laid off in 2025 as part of the Trump administration’s mass staffing cuts. Still, her name appeared on letters sent from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality — an office within HHS tasked with overseeing how Americans get care — nine months after she was let go.

Virtually no grant officers remain at the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. Over the summer, the Trump administration abruptly canceled at least 150 grants issued through the office, and now top political appointees won’t tell Congress where they’re redirecting those millions of dollars.

“We are trying to fulfill our obligation as grantees of the government and we can’t even do that right now,” Eric Roberts, a health economist at the University of Pennsylvania studying how to improve insurance coverage for people on both Medicare and Medicaid, told The Washington Sun.

Roberts last heard from his program officer on Aug. 14, 2025. He texted the officer in January; his message was marked as “read” but he didn’t get a response.

Then, this July, Roberts — like dozens of other grantees — received a letter saying his grant had been terminated. He told The Washington Sun he hasn’t been able to file a final report on his findings because his grant is still marked “pending” on the portal.

The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality was once staffed by around 280, but more than 120 employees were let go in July 2025, including nearly all the grant officers.

Staffing continued to decline over the past year as employees left and weren’t replaced. The officers who manage relationships with grantees, shepherding their applications, ushering them through the peer review process and overseeing their work, were let go.

At the time of the firings, grantees — who study topics like preventing hospital-acquired infections or improving cardiovascular care — received emails saying the agency was unable to process awards and that future awards were uncertain. Then, over the past year, some were ghosted by grant officers, who stopped responding to emails and text messages.

Nora Becker, a professor of internal medicine at the University of Michigan, said she wasn’t able to submit the final paperwork on the portal after her grant was canceled. She said the university’s grants staff decided to just email the final paperwork to a general email address at AHRQ.

“Insanity,” Becker wrote in an email.

And an unusual signature is on funding notices for grantees whose awards are continuing. While they would normally be signed by George Gardner, AHRQ’s grants director, recent notices have instead been signed by Kimberly Pendleton Chew, who works in the Food and Drug Administration’s grants division.

The health care research and quality office has emerged as a focal point for Democrats and health advocates who say the Trump administration isn’t being forthcoming about how it’s managing congressionally appropriated funds with a skeletal staff and has rescinded grant money that is now virtually untrackable.

“It appears that AHRQ is being intentionally run into the ground through a combination of incompetence and disregard for the law, and something needs to change,” Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin) told deputy health secretary nominee Chris Klomp at his confirmation hearing in September.

About two-thirds of AHRQ’s grant dollars for 2026 are publicly unaccounted for, even though the agency’s director, Roger Klein, told a court this month almost all had been spent. AHRQ leaders have told the office of Sen. Patty Murray (D-Washington) they are transferring the dollars to other agencies, including the National Institutes of Health, but haven’t released documents detailing exactly how.

This month, a congressional watchdog declared that the agency broke federal law by failing to spend all of its 2025 funds without notifying Congress of the changes. Baldwin and Murray wrote to the agency in September, asking it to detail how it’s spending the grant funds.

“I really don’t understand it. These are not state secrets, these are not things that are supposed to be kept under wraps,” said Aaron Carroll, president of AcademyHealth, a nonprofit representing health policy researchers that tracks AHRQ’s activities closely.

HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard said that “AHRQ has engaged in innovative, meaningful research and quality partnerships with other agencies” as part of its congressional appropriation but didn’t provide more details about where the grant money is going.

Congress created the agency in 1989 because people were getting very different medical care depending on where they lived. Its job was to fund research on how good health care is, what it costs, how well it works and who can get it.

The agency is now operating with about 70 staffers — about 25% of its usual workforce. At the same time, it has added political appointees. It used to have just one: the director.

Besides Klein, political appointees now include senior advisor Christina Chacon, chief of staff Erica Moshtahedian and senior advisor Tammy Born Huizenga, who has been charged with advancing priorities of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again initiative.

Kennedy highlighted AHRQ in his weekly email update to HHS employees sent Oct. 20 but made only a passing mention of its research work, instead focusing on its oversight of a preventive services task force and some surveys the agency conducts.

Congress gave AHRQ $215 million for research grants in 2026. While the agency typically awards about 400 new or ongoing grants annually, it has told Murray’s office it intends to fund just 90 this year. Last year, it funded one new grant and 206 ongoing grants.

“If they really have spent all the money, they should be able to show their work and show their work publicly,” said Stephanie Garlock, an attorney at Public Citizen, the progressive watchdog/advocacy group that is suing the administration over changes to AHRQ’s grant program.

The agency has said what it’s doing with some of the funds. About $30 million is being used on a joint initiative with the National Institutes of Health to make school lunches healthier. Another $7.5 million will go to sepsis management for the Indian Health Service. The agency is also awarding around $20 million in a competition for innovators that predated this administration.

But that leaves tens of millions of dollars publicly unaccounted for.

The Government Accountability Office ruled this month that HHS violated the federal impoundment act when it withheld 2025 funds from obligation and expenditure after announcing a reduction in force, without submitting a special message to Congress.

“There are researchers who invested a lot of effort, time and money into their projects and they don’t know if they’ll ever get results,” Garlock said.

entries.title: Is There a Reason There Are So Many Dan Sullivans in Alaska? An Investigation.
entries.summary: Alaska’s unusual demographics could explain part of its Dan glut in state politics.
entries.content:
Alaska has two men named Dan Sullivan on the ballot for Senate. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, the sitting Republican senator, has been endorsed by a third Dan Sullivan, the former mayor of Anchorage.

Having multiple Dan Sullivans on the ballot has already created serious issues for the election. The Trump administration has preemptively lined up a challenge to Alaska’s results should the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan lose. The other Dan Sullivan running is only doing so “for the purpose of confusing or misleading voters,” the Justice Department alleges.

But all this got us thinking: Is there a reason Alaska has so many Dans Sullivan?

Let’s approach the data systematically.

At birth, Daniel — by far the most common Dan variant to appear on birth certificates — hasn’t been unusually popular in Alaska, Social Security Administration data shows. In recent decades, Daniel has, if anything, been less common up there than in the nation at large.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Tqt5H/2/While Social Security’s privacy rules make it tough to look beyond Daniel, other metrics allowed us to include Dan and Dannys, as well as alternate spellings thereof. We excluded Danas, Danes and Dantes on the advice of resident expert and Sun columnist Dana Milbank, who’s never been a Dan in his life.

These sources show Alaska once had a proud Dan tradition. A sample from the 1930 Census showed the territory was home to twice as many Dans as the national average rate, while WWII enlistment files show Dans holding strong at 1.8 times the national rate. One of the few sources of contemporary names, FEC donor files from the past two decades, suggest the state remains well-endowed, Danwise. It’s got about 16% more Dans than you’d expect, putting it in 4th place among all states.

How can that be, given the state’s quotidian Daniel birth rate?

Well, Alaska’s adult male population is unusual. It has, proportionally, the most men of any state in the union.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/wcHJc/1/Thanks to military bases, oil fields and other male-dominated workplaces, Alaska just happens to have, pound for pound, more men ages 20 to 44 than any other state.
DANSULLIVAN.png (3034x2325, AR: 1.30)And it just so happens the name Daniel peaked in popularity about 40 years ago, giving Alaska the most Dan-friendly population profile of any state.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BrAJK/2/Most of those men came from elsewhere. And it turns out, many came from America’s Dan belt — particularly California, the second-most-Daniel-heavy state and the biggest source of out-of-state Alaskans.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/RwPgU/1/Now let’s talk about the Alaska Sullivans.

Our estimates varied by source but, if anything, the state has fewer Sullivans than the national average — an average pushed up pretty high by Massachusetts and its New England neighbors.

But it doesn’t take that many Sullivans to generate a bumper crop of Dan Sullivans. Male Sullivans are several times more likely to be named Dan than the non-Sullivan males, a fact you can perhaps blame on the Catholic Daniels and, perhaps, a few Gaelic Domhnalls who preferred not to go by Donald.

You get an additional boost from the fact that Dans and Sullivans are a bit more likely to be in politics than folks with other first and last names (by exactly how much depends on the age group you’re looking at).

But while you can get cute with numbers — and we do! — in reality, the Dan logjam is almost certainly a coincidence in the sparsely populated far-flung state.

That said, if you were drafting states in which men named Dan Sullivan would dominate politics, you’d probably pick Alaska in the early rounds.

entries.title: D.C. United Wants Public Money to Expand Audi Field. It’s Not an Easy Goal.
entries.summary: The team says more seats and a roof would allow more events, but the path through the D.C. Council could be complicated.
entries.content:
In recent years, D.C. taxpayers have committed $515 million to renovate the Capital One Arena and more than $1 billion to help build a new stadium for the Washington Commanders, as well as agreeing to putting the proceeds from a business tax to finance a $400 million renovation of Nationals Park — itself built with taxpayer dollars.

But is a request for hundreds of millions of dollars to add 8,000 seats and a new roof to D.C. United’s Audi Field — constructed in part with public funds just over a decade ago — one ask too many? Or is it a justifiable investment in a venue that hosts a global sport and growing roster of teams?

That question is now percolating through the Wilson Building, as D.C. lawmakers debate the extent of their continued investment in sports facilities in a city that markets itself as the “Sports Capital” but is facing uncertain economic times.

In July, D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson quietly introduced legislation that would commit $300 million in public funding — split up over five years — to the expansion of Audi Field, with D.C. United kicking in $320 million of its own. The money would go towards additional seating, a roof and more than 400 units of housing on an empty parcel of land adjacent to the stadium.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Reactions to the proposal have broken down along the usual lines: Proponents say it would bring more people to Audi Field for more events and generate economic activity for the surrounding Buzzard Point area, while critics argue that the claims of economic benefits are overstated and that D.C. shouldn’t be committing any more public money to stadiums and arenas — especially as lawmakers face the prospect of cutting programs and services.

But the bill has also scrambled the usual politics around putting public dollars into professional sports facilities. Mendelson — often a skeptic of the practice — is the main proponent, while Mayor Muriel Bowser, who negotiated public funding deals for the Capitals, Wizards and Commanders, has spoken out against it.

The Washington Spirit are also an unexpected X factor: The popular women’s team is unhappy with their current lease with D.C. United, and want to use the bill as leverage to negotiate a deal that makes them more of a partner than a renter of the space.

“I’m of two minds about the proposal,” said Ward 6 council member Charles Allen, who represents the neighborhood where Audi Field is located, during a daylong hearing Friday. “On one hand, when I view this proposal as a District resident and taxpayer, I feel uneasy, especially since this is coming on the heels of the RFK Campus redevelopment. On the other hand … I see the amount of economic activity the stadium is able to generate by hosting D.C. United and Washington Spirit games.”

The potential of the latter is what proponents are putting forth to ease concerns over the former.

“Nearly two decades ago, Nationals Park became the catalyst and center of gravity for the Navy Yard. The ballpark drew people, and the grocery stores, restaurants, parks and services residents now rely on, followed. Audi Field can play that role for Buzzard Point,” said Emeka Moneme, president of the Navy Yard Business Improvement District. “On match days, foot traffic in Buzzard Point runs 12 to 14 times that of a typical non-event day. Seven shops and restaurants now operate in Buzzard Point, and when the stadium is dark, they feel it.”

D.C. United officials say adding a roof and more seats — capacity is currently 19,200, and it would increase to around 28,000 — would dramatically increase the number of games and events Audi Field could hold.

It would also facilitate Major League Soccer’s move to a new schedule in early 2028 — aimed at better aligning with European leagues — but also expand opportunities for concerts, festivals and other teams at the stadium, including the Washington Spirit and the D.C. Flight, a brand new professional women’s volleyball team. (D.C. Power FC, another women’s soccer team, also plays at Audi Field, as do the D.C. Defenders, a United Football League team.)

“When we look at the roof project, it’s not just comparing it to the soccer landscape. We’re looking at the broader mission of becoming a sports capital, to serve our clients and bring in more events as we become more of a year-round facility,” said Danita Johnson, D.C. United’s president of business operations.

But Shira Markoff, the director of economic policy for the liberal D.C. Fiscal Policy Institute, argued that while a bigger and roofed Audi Field may be able to host more events, that’s not reason enough for public funds to be used on the upgrades.

“Economic research shows that sports stadiums are not significant drivers of local economic growth,” she said.

One marquee critic of the proposed deal for the soccer stadium was Nina Albert, D.C.’s deputy mayor for planning and economic development. She defended the city’s investments in the Capital One Arena, Nationals Park and the new Commanders stadium, but argued that Audi Field isn’t old enough to merit the public outlay — for now.

“We must be clear-eyed about what investments are necessary, when the best time is for making those investments, and what we need to know before committing more than $300 million in public funds,” she said. “A $300 million investment merits study, I don’t think that’s unreasonable.”

Albert added that one of Bowser’s principal concerns is that whatever events a larger Audi Field could attract — primarily concerts — would “cannibalize” Capital One Arena, though proponents of the deal countered that there’s enough demand to satisfy what both venues could offer artists.

Ultimately, the path to a deal for D.C. United and Audi Field may have to pass through the Spirit, which has played at the stadium since 2023 and is in the process of renegotiating its lease.

Though team CEO Kim Stone told lawmakers that the Spirit are “neutral” on the bill, in recent weeks they made clear that they want to use any possible legislation as leverage to negotiate better terms, including distinct signage, their own locker room, and certainty that the women’s team won’t get short-shrifted during what would likely be a two-year construction period that could displace home games.

“We believe in the value of Audi Field, but the details need to be refined in order to make sure we have enforceable protections that are good for everyone,” Stone said.

The Spirit’s quiet lobbying seems to have paid dividends. “It’s very hard for us to be supportive if you’re not able to bring the Spirit on-side,” Ward 3 council member Matt Frumin told D.C. United officials at the hearing. “I am in principle supportive of this, but that is going to be a prerequisite.”

What happens next — and when — remains up in the air. D.C. United CEO Jason Levien said that with the MLS schedule change set to take effect in January 2028 and negotiations ongoing with the Spirit, he’d like lawmakers to move as quickly as possible to give some certainty after what he says was years of lobbying for the project.

“I'm really worried that if we don't have it done by December, I wouldn't say all hope is lost, because I don't like to lose hope, but I think I worry about how we keep the Spirit, how we keep the other tenants happy, and how we prepare Audi Field for the change in the calendar,” he said.

In a statement to The Sun, the Spirit said while a new lease is a “top priority,” the team is “committed” to staying in D.C.

D.C. United has already started sweetening the pot for lawmakers, announcing it has already agreed in principle to work with labor unions on construction of the expanded stadium and neighboring housing project. These project labor agreements have often been points of contention in other D.C. stadium deals.

Still, Levien’s hopeful timeline might be faster than some lawmakers are ready to accept.

“It sounds like we need to do a lot more studying,” said At-Large council member Elissa Silverman. “It sounds like we’re a little premature in moving forward until we understand the impacts financially and on infrastructure.”

entries.title: A Catholic Republican 2028 Nominee Would Make History. Does Anyone Care?
entries.summary: Two likely 2028 candidates, JD Vance and Marco Rubio, are practicing Catholics, but their faith isn’t the political obstacle it was a generation ago.
entries.content:
For decades, Catholic politicians faced deep suspicion from evangelical Christians, a voting bloc that would eventually become the backbone of the Republican Party.

Now, if either Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio wins the 2028 nomination, they would become the first Catholic to lead a Republican presidential ticket. And hardly anyone seems to care about their religion.

The theological differences that once divided Catholics and evangelicals have given way to a political alliance built around opposition to abortion, LGBTQ+ rights and what both groups see as threats to religious freedom.

For Vance and Rubio, that means their faith is less of an obstacle to winning the Republican nomination than it would have been a generation ago.

“I don’t think, ‘Oh, he’s a Catholic,’ plays like it did 20, 30 years, 40 years ago,” Chad Connelly, the founder of Faith Wins, a pastor mobilization group, told The Washington Sun. “It’s policies.”

The change reflects a broader realignment in American politics, one where religious conservatives have found common ground across denominational lines.

“The ultimate divide today, sadly, is really between those who believe there is a God and choose to follow him and those who believe there isn't one,” said Eric Teetsel, the CEO and publisher of Chronicles magazine who served as the director of faith outreach for Rubio’s 2016 presidential campaign.

Even though conservative evangelicals may not care that Rubio or Vance are Catholic, they are deeply motivated by the social issues that the two men have spent their political careers espousing.

Their overt religiosity could also help distinguish them from President Donald Trump, who has maintained strong support among white evangelicals despite rarely engaging on the specifics of his own beliefs.

Trump’s particular lack of piety and his administration’s inaction on evangelical priorities has led operatives and activists to have concerns that Republicans overlooked evangelical voters while campaigning for the midterms. But Teetsel predicted that either Vance or Rubio would achieve greater enthusiasm among religious conservatives in 2028 than Trump has.

Spokespeople for Vance and Rubio did not respond to requests for comment.

It helps that Vance and Rubio tend to speak in a vocabulary that resonates with evangelical Christians. Vance was raised in a loosely evangelical environment, which often comes across in the way he talks about religion and how he cites the Bible. During a speech at the GOP midterm convention, he quoted the Book of Romans — the New Testament book that anchored much of the Protestant Reformation.

On a recent podcast with a popular Christian media personality, the vice president tackled questions commonly discussed in evangelical circles: Why do some lose faith? How can Christians reach the younger generation? What to do about hypocrisy in the church?

He used a salvation maxim heard most Sundays in both megachurches and wooden pews, of how “Jesus comes into your heart.”

Vance referred to sanctification — the process for a Christian to become more like Christ. It’s common throughout the faith but emphasized among evangelicals.

“For some people that's very quick, but for most people that's a process,” Vance said. “Grace is constantly working on people.”

Rubio’s own spiritual wandering — a Roman Catholic upbringing, a dalliance with Mormonism, a gaze at evangelicalism and an ultimate return to his childhood faith — helped his familiarity with the converging religious terms that have cross-pollinated among conservatives.

“Marco Rubio perfectly encapsulates what I think of as the sort of evange-Catholic nature of a lot of Americans, and that includes a lot of American political leaders,” Teetsel said. “They may align with something like the Catholic Church at the end of the day, but they're very fluent and comfortable in evangelical Protestant circles too.”

But if Vance faces resistance from evangelical voters, it may spring from an unexpected issue: Israel.

Connelly said that in his conversations with evangelical pastors, concerns about the vice president have little to do with his Catholicism and much more to do with his foreign policy views.

“I'm not hearing about Catholic faith,” Connelly said. “I'm hearing, ‘I think he's kind of squishy on Israel.’”

Support for Israel is deeply rooted in the theology of many evangelical Christians, particularly those who believe the modern state of Israel plays a role in biblical prophecy. For those voters, American support for Israel is not just a policy preference but a religious conviction.

Concerns around Vance’s commitment to Israel, and anti-interventionist tendencies, have also been compounded by his friendship with Tucker Carlson, the conservative media personality whose rhetoric around Israel and antisemitism has alienated many evangelicals.

“Most of them think Tucker Carlson's taken a hard-left turn or been demon possessed, for goodness sakes,” Connelly said.

Vance has defended his relationship with Carlson, arguing that political disagreements shouldn't require people to sever personal ties. He has also sought to reassure Jewish Republicans about his commitment to Israel, including in a recent appearance before the Republican Jewish Coalition.

For some evangelical voters, differences on foreign policy, especially between Vance and Rubio, could become a meaningful issue in a 2028 primary. But the fact that the concerns center on Israel rather than Catholic doctrine illustrates just how much the politics of religion have changed.

“We’ve moved past the fear that a Catholic politician is going to do the Vatican’s bidding from the Oval Office,” said Greg Scott, a conservative Protestant operative.

It wasn’t too long ago that the relationship was decidedly more toxic, resembling hostile allies rather than aligned minds.

One Catholic Republican operative recalled it being common on the campaign trail in the early 2010s to hear remarks that dismissed Catholics as being non-Christians — phrases like: Catholics aren’t Christians or You’re Catholic, I’m Christian. 

With the increase in Catholics holding high political offices came moments that exemplified the acceptance of Catholicism in American politics, particularly within conservative circles. Foremost was Pope Francis’ 2015 visit to the U.S. Capitol, organized by House Speaker John Boehner.

It wasn’t that one moment marked the breakthrough — aspects of the pope’s visit were roundly criticized by some conservative publications at the time. But eventually the sheer number of Catholics contributing to the conservative movement reached critical mass. Even for hesitant evangelicals, it was no longer tenable to hold a reflexively antagonistic position, the Catholic operative said.

“If you are an evangelical, you cannot really dispute the fact that the American Catholics have been reliable allies to you,” the Catholic operative said. “Maybe prejudice that you had, or maybe your parents or grandparents would have had, is not only unfounded but is also unproductive for your political aims.”
AP 25138359208803 (8417x5611, AR: 1.50)Although most experts agree that the beef between the groups is a nonfactor — “completely dead” is how Andrew T. Walker, dean of the School of Theology at the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary, described it — some said vestiges of old conflicts remain.

One evangelical political operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak candidly, told The Sun that the impact of any feud is muted, but it still has an effect on the margins. The operative said they knew of instances where some Republican Hill offices will occasionally filter out Catholics when hiring, while other offices filter out Protestants.

The gradual migration of Roman Catholics to conservatism coincided with their mass exodus from the Democratic Party, despite Democrats’ track record of elevating Catholic leaders. The only presidents to hold the faith — John F. Kennedy and Joe Biden — were Democrats. So was the first Catholic speaker of the House, John W. McCormack. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi has been outspoken about her Catholicism but faced backlash for pushing abortion-rights legislation, including an edict from the archbishop of San Francisco that she would be denied Communion for her abortion position.

Catholics have increasingly swung toward the GOP in recent elections: Trump won 55% of the Catholic vote to Kamala Harris’ 43%. That gulf widens when looking at voters who, like Vance himself, converted to Catholicism.

Among converted Catholics, 59% identified as Republicans compared to 33% as Democrats, according to a report from the Tufts Public Opinion Lab. Republicans also had a larger share among those who grew up Catholic, but by a significantly lower margin — 48% to 44%.

“The most highly contested political issues basically boil down to Genesis 1,” Teetsel said. “There's either God's created order, the nature of male and female, the meaning of marriage, the dignity of life, or there isn't. And what we see is the political parties have broken down on opposite lines of those most fundamental questions.”

A recent poll hinted at another twist, however: a drop in support for Vance among Catholics. Following spats with Pope Leo XIV, a Navigator Research survey found Vance’s net favorability almost 70 percentage points lower than the pope’s.

It’s another indication that Vance, specifically, could be a unique test case for the mood of religion on the right.

In the early weeks of the Iran war, Pope Leo asserted that God doesn’t bless conflict. The comment caused Trump, predictably, to lash out at him. Vance sided with Trump, saying the pope should stick with what’s happening in the Catholic Church.

Vance suggested later that the pope should “be careful” when he speaks of theology to make sure “it’s anchored in the truth”; a bold complaint from a devout Catholic who had met Pope Leo and had defended him from some on the right after the pope’s election.

Last Wednesday, Vance shared his continued prayers for the pope to recover from his cancer diagnosis. The back-and-forth exemplifies the tension of Vance’s position: trying to be a political attack dog one day and give a Gospel discourse the next.

Rubio and other potential candidates, like Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri), have used their religion to bring people into the party, the evangelical operative said. But Vance can use his religion to attack his opponents — even when his criticism is directed at the actual pope.

One trait of that attack-dog mentality has troubled some Republican Christians: Vance likes to say “shit.” Literally, he says “shit.” A lot.

The vice president has often ascribed his salty tongue to his Appalachian upbringing, as a quirk of social class. But it continues to bother those less inclined to pardon his French.

Politicians cussing is a trend. Most of the people employing it, however, don’t do book tours about their journeys into Christendom. To see Vance as their guy, some need him to stop spewing the foul language.

“It might not come down to these religious things,” the evangelical operative said. But if it does, “even something so much as how much he swears is going to matter on the margins.”

“Every time he curses,” they added, “I just think it looks unpresidential.”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Football Players of Week 9
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts include a dynamic quarterback from South Lakes and a lockdown defensive back from Gonzaga.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

With the postseason right around the corner, the clock is ticking for the DMV’s top football programs. Here are five players who stood out in a wild week:

Wilton Cameron, Senior, Athlete, Blake

Cameron stepped up late to help Blake earn a rivalry victory Thursday over Paint Branch in Silver Spring. The senior, who plays quarterback on offense for the Bengals, called his own number deep in the second half and burst free for a 30-yard rushing touchdown run to give coach Bryon Marshall’s team a late edge.

He finished the job as a defensive back moments later. Cameron extinguished the Panthers’ last gasp effort in the fourth quarter by tipping a pass to a teammate for the game-sealing interception.

“That win was very important for us and for the program, and also for my teammates to give them the edge to never give up,” Cameron said. “That game should keep us going to win [the rest of the season] and try to get us to the state championship, which is our goal.”

Darius Knight, Senior, Running Back, Dunbar

Saturday’s D.C. public school bout between Dunbar and Theodore Roosevelt was a battle between two of the most potent offenses in the city. Knight led the charge at running back for the Crimson Tide — the senior rushed for over 100 yards and four touchdowns in an eventual 34-19 victory.

Coach Maurice Vaughn’s offense eclipsed 30 points for the third time in four weeks and are hitting their stride with the DCIAA playoffs approaching.

“Darius is our bell cow,” Vaughn said. “We’re going to go as far as he takes us.”

Matthew Larsen, Senior, Quarterback, Sherwood

Larsen has been a steadying presence at quarterback for a Warriors team that’s been plagued by injuries this fall. Despite being down four top receiving targets to injury, Larsen captained Sherwood to a dramatic 34-29 win against Damascus on Friday. The senior completed 21 of his 30 passes for 257 yards and a touchdown, including a late 56-yard strike in the fourth quarter to give the Warriors a late lead.

Larsen, a four-year starter for the Sandy Spring program, threw his 77th career touchdown pass in the victory as the Warriors moved to 7-1.

Jackson Waddy, Junior, Defensive Back, Gonzaga

Waddy is one of several strong defensive weapons for the Eagles, who held WCAC rival Good Counsel out of the end zone in a 21-3 victory over the Falcons on Friday. Waddy nabbed an interception, five solo tackles and a pass breakup for coach Randy Trivers’ defense, a unit that has given up just 9 points in the last two weeks against capable conference competition.

“Our defense played solid all around, making sure we neutralized the run game,” Trivers said. “We were really able to do a good job of eliminating Good Counsel’s big plays.”

Christian Wyatt, Senior, Quarterback, South Lakes

In a matchup between two of the most potent offenses in Northern Virginia, Wyatt exploded for five total touchdowns for South Lakes in a 40-28 win over Madison. The senior quarterback passed for 261 yards and two touchdowns — both of which were hauled by junior wide receiver Joshua-Benjamin Dagbe, who racked up 156 yards and three total touchdowns in the victory.

Wyatt added three more scores on the ground as coach Jason Hescock’s team emerged victorious in the shootout win.

“[Wyatt] is definitely not selfish giving that ball around,” Hescock said. “He called his own number a couple of times, called a bunch of other guys’ numbers a bunch of times. … It’s really nice that he’s on our team and we don’t have to gameplan for him.”

entries.title: D.C. Dispensary Consumption Spaces Are Rising Social Hubs
entries.summary: With drinking on the decline, people are finding community within cannabis dispensary walls.
entries.content:
On a Friday evening in Adams Morgan, about two dozen people gathered inside a cannabis dispensary to watch drag queens perform.

Many smoked. Others chatted over drinks — nonalcoholic ones — while Sapphica Star and Lexxus Star performed at Blunt Sluts, a dispensary that has become more than a storefront. To the right of the sales counter is the “giggle room,” an event space where customers can use cannabis products.

The drag show is one of a growing number of events at D.C. dispensaries that are aimed at building communities around cannabis consumption, from “puff and pilates” to comedy shows.

Blunt Sluts’ co-owner Shelby Fountain said the events grew organically from conversations with customers. “They started forming their own kind of community,” she said.

Blunt Sluts and Higher Ground, a Northeast D.C. dispensary, both operate consumption spaces where customers can use cannabis on-site while attending events. Other dispensaries around the city are experimenting with similar models.

D.C.’s cannabis consumption spaces were made possible by a law that went into effect in 2023, creating a safe-use treatment facility endorsement that allows licensed medical cannabis retailers to offer on-site consumption areas for patients.

Customers and employees at the dispensaries said the appeal is largely about giving people an alternative to the traditional bar.

“What's wrong with the little joint at the end of the day?” Fountain said. “I mean, it's kind of like our glass of wine, honestly. It's just something social to bring us all together and talk about our days and personal lives and other things.”

That dynamic was on display at the Blunt Sluts drag show. Sapphica Star said some people enjoy queer nightlife but may not want to spend an evening in a packed, loud bar.

“The people that come to this event are people who are really genuine, down to earth,” Sapphica Star said. “I think everyone's looking for community and looking to connect on a deeper level.”
Blunt Sluts drag show (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)The shift comes as alcohol consumption has been declining among U.S. adults.

Gallup reported in August that only 54% of American adults said they drink alcohol, matching the record-low level measured in 2025. The share stood at 67% in 2022.

Fountain described the “Cali sober” lifestyle — abstaining from alcohol and other substances while continuing to use cannabis — as increasingly visible among her customers.

“There are people who come into Blunt Sluts all the time who have just bad incidents with alcohol or bad memories or associations,” she said. “A lot of people are just trying to get away from alcohol in general.”

Sapphica Star, who said she stopped drinking, said younger people are increasingly questioning the traditional drinking-centered nightlife model.

“There are reasons that contain multitudes for why our generation has sort of abandoned the notion of the party drinking culture and sort of embraced weed,” Sapphica Star said, pointing to the effects of alcohol and its rising cost.

The shift is also visible at Higher Ground.

“People are still looking for social stuff to do,” said Robbie Martin, the dispensary’s general manager and president of the D.C. Cannabis Business Association. He boiled the question down to: “If I'm going to drink less, where can I still find social things to go out and do?”

Higher Ground, which soft-opened in January and began hosting events in April, is trying to answer that question.

The dispensary hosts magic shows as well as yoga and sound bath classes. Martin said the goal is to make the space appealing even to people who might not consider themselves stereotypical cannabis consumers.

“It's not just ‘Hey, I have to be a stoner to go to Higher Ground,’” Martin said. “We want to put on enough different varieties of community events that enough people see this as a home base.”
Robbie Martin (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)That idea is also attracting people from the hospitality industry who are looking for an alternative to serving alcohol. Martin said many of the people involved with Higher Ground came from hospitality and nightlife backgrounds.

Clint Leonard, who works as a budtender at Higher Ground, is one of those people.

“I've been a cannabis user for a long time, and so I thought that my skills in hospitality could transition to a place like this really well,” Leonard said.

At Higher Ground, he said, the same skills that make a bar or restaurant function — welcoming customers, creating an atmosphere and fostering conversation — can be applied to dispensaries.

“We are cultivating here a community space that can be used in a lot of the same ways that a bar venue could be used or a restaurant venue could be used, but obviously just without the alcohol aspect,” Leonard said.

Higher Ground is also trying to make cannabis itself part of the experience. The business grows cannabis on-site, allowing customers to see the plants behind the products they consume.

“To be able to put somebody at that bar, and they're five feet away from 300 plants, is a really unique opportunity for education and to just normalize the conversation as a whole,” he said.

The concept is spreading beyond the two businesses.

Blunt Sluts recently opened another location in Capitol Hill. Wash Hydro in Adams Morgan operates a consumption space that customers can rent hourly or access through an annual $420 pass. Love 420, which opened near Nationals Park in September, plans to offer four private consumption spaces.

“It's food, it's music, it's arts, it's culture — and that's really the driver behind that,” Martin said. “We feel strongly that cannabis does live in all of these different communities. There just hasn't really been a venue for that gathering.”
