entries.title: Catholic Leaders Feel ‘Manipulated’ and ‘Exploited’ After Trump’s Oval Office Photo Op
entries.summary: “I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple,” one bishop wrote.
entries.content:
Catholic leaders who were photographed last week praying with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office said they felt “manipulated” and “exploited” by the way the meeting was publicized.

In a 30-second clip of the interaction, a group of bishops and archbishops stand over the president and pray following a policy meeting with Trump and White House staff.

But the clip was quickly blasted out on social media by Trump’s campaign account, with the caption: “Catholic Archbishops and Bishops gather in the Oval Office to pray with President @realDonaldTrump.”

The meeting was scheduled months ago by the White House Faith Office to discuss a range of policy matters including immigration, abortion and federal tax credits for private education, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines wrote. It was not, he said, intended to be a political endorsement.

After speaking with the president, the bishops and archbishops were invited to pray with him, a relatively routine request of faith leaders of all denominations. It was the second of two meetings that the president has held with faith leaders, according to Denver Archbishop James Golka.
https://x.com/TrumpWarRoom/status/2113348041692356736Golka told the Denver Catholic that while he thought the meeting was private, he always knew it could be made public.

“I understand that many people saw the video, posted by the administration 12 days before an election, as an endorsement,” Golka said. “That was never my intention.”

Joenson also put out a statement saying he regretted how the interaction was used by the White House without permission to signal Catholic leaders’ support for Trump.

“I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes,” Joensen wrote. “I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward.”

A third Catholic leader to speak out following the meeting, Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, went further, writing a public apology on Sunday, saying the group had no idea that a video was taken, and the White House never asked for permission to publicly post videos and photos of the meeting.

“I feel a heavy sadness, not only over the pain I caused, but also for the fact that something so sacred to a group of religious leaders, prayer to our Heavenly Father, would be manipulated in that way,” Grob wrote.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers wrote that “there has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump.”

“His strong record proves it,” she said.

entries.title: Trump Confirms He’s ‘Thinking About’ Booting Reporters From the White House
entries.summary: The president, however, contested reports that he plans to build a swimming pool in the briefing room.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump appeared to confirm that he is considering relocating the press from the White House in a record-breaking post on Truth Social.

When comedian Bill Maher had former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt on his “Real Time” show Friday, she indicated that Trump had been “flirting” with turning the briefing room into a swimming pool.

But Trump’s 1,300-word Truth Social tirade against Maher Sunday evening appeared to rule out the possibility of returning the space to its original purpose — while confirming that he is mulling whether to remove the press from the White House entirely, as reports indicated last week.

“I am not building a swimming pool in the White House Briefing Room, and never had any intention of doing so,” Trump wrote Sunday night in the post, his longest ever on the platform. “I am thinking about moving the Press, and putting them in a different location, but I will use that location for very badly needed space.”

The White House referred The Washington Sun to Trump’s post when asked about any plans to relocate the press and reimagine the briefing room.

Maher, who Trump called a “COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER,” is the latest member of the media to draw the fury of the president. Maher went to the White House for a dinner with Trump earlier this month, but he proceeded to criticize the administration and point out Trump’s low approval rating.

The media has increasingly come under fire during Trump’s second term. In recent weeks, Trump has called one journalist a “dummy,” another “a stupid person” and a third “a sick person.”

The White House is currently locked in ongoing litigation with three news outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — that had their press passes revoked in September at Trump’s direction, a decision that effectively banned them from White House grounds. The administration quickly appealed an Oct. 13 injunction in the case that reinstated their access, but some journalists have still been restricted from traveling with the president aboard Air Force One. (The Washington Sun has signed onto an amicus brief filed in support of the news outlets.)

The New York Times reported last week that Trump had pitched Leavitt on the idea of moving the press corps out of the briefing room in August, telling aides he was in favor of bringing back a swimming pool for the space. The Eisenhower Executive Office Building next to the West Wing could serve as a new base for credentialed media, the Times reported.

entries.title: Texas' First Post-Roe Report on Maternal Mortality Will Come After the Midterms
entries.summary: Democrats accused state Republicans of holding back the report because of the election.
entries.content:
Texas Democratic lawmakers have waited years for data showing how the state’s near-total abortion ban affected maternal mortality numbers across the state. They’ll have to keep waiting.

So will voters.

State officials have pushed the release of a biennial report that analyzes the deaths of pregnant women in Texas, saying they hope to release it by the start of December — long past the date it was originally anticipated to come out, and weeks after Election Day.

It will be the first report containing data after Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022, and Democrats have been quick to accuse state officials of holding it back for political reasons as Republican candidates in the state face competitive challenges.

“If the data came out and indicated that we are actually seeing more women who want their pregnancies are having complications, not getting the care that they need and even dying, that could get the attention of Republican women,” said Donna Howard, a Democrat who chairs the Texas Women's Health Caucus in the statehouse. “[They] would very likely say, ‘You’ve gone too far, and you haven’t done enough.’”

Democrats in the state have urged the release of the report.

“Texans deserve full transparency about the maternal mortality crisis plaguing our state and country — including the release of the Department of State Health Services report,” said JT Ennis, a spokesperson for James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in the state’s U.S. Senate race.

The report has typically been released no later than the start of September. As recently as March, members of the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Review Committee acknowledged during a public meeting that they were working to meet that deadline. But state officials have seized on a state law passed in 2025 that extends the deadline for some health-related reports to Dec. 1 as part of a broader effort to streamline the state’s health agency publication process.

The author of that bill, Democrat Rep. Christian Manuel, told the Texas Observer he believes the extended deadline provision has been “weaponized to withhold information” from the public.

The information in the report could be powerful in motivating voters in the state, where a key Senate race is playing out between Talarico and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Several House districts are also competitive, as is the governor’s race, where Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is facing unusually tight competition as he seeks a fourth term.

His opponent, Gina Hinojosa, has criticized the report’s delay.

“Greg Abbott delayed the release of the Maternal Mortality Report until after the election because he knows the results will be damning,” Hinojosa said in a statement to The Washington Sun.

As governor, Abbott has executive power over the Department of State Health Services and is able to appoint leadership and issue directives that guide policy enforcement.

In statements provided to The Sun, Abbott’s office and the Department of State Health Services denied that the report has been held back.

“There is no delay. Under HB 4666, which the Texas Legislature passed in an overwhelmingly bipartisan fashion, the deadline for DSHS to submit the report is Dec. 1,” said Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary, in a statement to The Sun.

The DSHS pointed to the same deadline.

The report “is proceeding through the DSHS internal review process,” a spokesperson for the department said in a statement. “As part of that process, the acting commissioner has asked the committee to strengthen the report by further describing its work around preventability, better defining the sources of its recommendations, and making clearer connections between the underlying data, findings, and recommendations.” The statement went on to say the agency is working through the revisions “with the goal” of releasing it by Dec. 1.

Alina Salganicoff, the director of Women’s Health Policy program at KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research organization, told The Sun that it’s “unclear” why Texas’ report would need additional time to be completed, and “other states are pretty routinely doing this type of analysis to address” the deaths of pregnant patients.

The biennial maternal mortality report has been delayed once before. In 2022, the release was similarly held until December, after Election Day had passed. Once released, the report, which analyzed deaths from the year 2019, before Texas’ abortion ban was in place, showed an increase in deaths of pregnant Black women.

While there is not yet state data to show how Texas’ abortion bans may have affected the deaths of pregnant patients, media outlets have reported instances of delayed care for some women. ProPublica has identified at least four pregnant Texas women who died in the year after the state’s abortion ban went into effect because they were denied care while experiencing pregnancy complications.

The number of women who have died after experiencing ectopic pregnancies spiked nationally following the Dobbs decision, further ProPublica reporting has found. The likelihood of death is nearly twice as high in states with abortion bans, the outlet found.

“Nobody wants to be the party of women dying,” said Lauren Peterson, the CEO of Abortion in America, an abortion advocacy organization whose legal arm is suing the state on behalf of the family of a woman who died after being denied abortion care. “If I were a politician who had advocated for the state’s abortion ban, I would surely not want people hearing these stories.”

entries.title: Trump’s Press Ban Faces a New Legal Challenge From a Group of Citizens
entries.summary: “The ultimate injury here … is to the democratic public,” the lawsuit argues.
entries.content:
By Jocelyn Noveck

In the increasingly bitter legal standoff between President Donald Trump and media outlets whose reporting he dislikes, a new and crucial third party has emerged: citizens who watch and read the news and need it to do their jobs.

A lawsuit filed Monday on behalf of six such citizens — effectively representing the audiences for the news media — argues that it’s not only the rights of news organizations that are violated when Trump bans them from White House premises. Even more fundamentally, the lawsuit argues, such bans violate the public’s right to independent reporting about its president and government.

“The ultimate injury here … is to the democratic public,” says the suit, filed in federal district court in New York against Trump and three key aides, including the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles.

“The First Amendment protects the public’s right to know what its government is doing,” said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute, which filed the lawsuit on behalf of the six plaintiffs, along with the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School.

“The White House cannot decide what information Americans receive by punishing critical reporting," Fallow said in a statement. "When the White House expels reporters because of their coverage and threatens others with expulsion, it isn’t just the press that suffers — the public loses access to independent reporting and gets something closer to government propaganda.”

The plaintiffs all rely on White House news for their work

The six plaintiffs are all people who say they rely on independent and diverse White House reporting for their teaching, journalism or advocacy. They include a noted human rights advocate, a political journalist, a Yale history professor, a high school civics teacher, a legal journalist, and a student journalist at the University of Pennsylvania.

The complaint filed Monday recounts how various news organizations that have been targeted by Trump are already battling the administration in the courts. These cases include the current lawsuit by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, whose journalists were banished from the White House in September.

A ederal judge recently extended an order preventing the White House from enforcing the ban while the case makes its way through the legal system. Still affected, though, is CNN’s pool coverage of Trump. The White House has been denying the network its usual slots in the video pool covering the president’s activities and travel, and CNN has threatened further action.

Also continuing is the legal case involving The Associated Press, whose reporters were barred last year from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events in retaliation for the outlet’s decision not to follow Trump’s lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, to the Gulf of America.

The New York Times is also involved in litigation, over a Pentagon policy requiring escorts for journalists on its grounds. And ABC is fighting back against the Trump administration in a dispute over renewal of its broadcast licenses.

This lawsuit seeks more wide-ranging relief

The new lawsuit filed Monday, though, is different from previous legal action against the president — first, in that the plaintiffs are ordinary citizens. And it seeks more wide-ranging relief.

The suit, which names Trump as defendant along with Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, and Secret Service Director Sean M. Curran, calls not only for reinstatement of access that has already been impacted, but for a broad injunction that would protect from retaliation every news outlet that covers the White House.

The complaint says: “Defendants' policy of restricting the access of disfavored news organizations deprives the public of the reporting of those organizations, and it inevitably deprives them of the independent reporting of other news organizations as well, since every journalist who reports from the White House must now account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked."

“Plaintiffs ... seek a declaration that the policy is unconstitutional because it imposes restrictions on a limited public forum that are viewpoint-based and unreasonable. They also seek an injunction barring defendants from enforcing the policy.”

Plaintiffs include a human rights advocate, a teacher and a student journalist

The plaintiffs are:
  • Kenneth Roth, former longtime executive director of Human Rights Watch and a lecturer at Yale’s law school and school of global affairs. Roth “relies on newsgathering and reporting from members of the White House press corps to inform his public writing and commentary," the suit says.
  • —Daniel Froomkin, media and political journalist and editor of Press Watch, a nonprofit that encourages political journalists to “fulfill their essential mission of creating an informed electorate and holding the powerful accountable.”
  • Beverly Gage, Pulitzer Prize-winning historian and professor at Yale University who “relies on newsgathering and reporting from the White House press corps to inform her scholarship, public writing and commentary.”
  • Peter Schmidt-Nowara, a social studies teacher at a New York City high school, who teaches civics courses and considers White House reporting “essential to his work as an educator.”
  • Benjamin Wittes, editor-in-chief of Lawfare and a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, whose publication is “especially reliant on the White House press corps to provide accurate and timely coverage of the president.”
  • Ethan Young, a student at the University of Pennsylvania and editor-in-chief of The Daily Pennsylvanian, who, as a student journalist, “relies on a diverse, independent and trustworthy cohort of White House reporters to serve as his proxy.”
Schmidt-Nowara, who teaches at Brooklyn Technical High School, is quoted in the lawsuit as saying: “As a social studies teacher, I want my students to have access to accurate, independent reporting about their government." He adds he is "gravely concerned that the Trump administration’s restrictions on White House reporters are cutting off access to crucial information.

“I joined this lawsuit because my students deserve to know what’s happening in their government and to hear from a free and independent press,” he says.

Young, the student journalist, contends that since he can’t personally access White House press spaces, he relies on “a diverse, independent and trustworthy cohort” of White House reporters to serve as his proxy.

The effect of federal policy changes has been "acutely felt on college campuses, Penn’s included,” Young is quoted as saying. “As a student journalist, I rely on reporting from the White House press corps to understand the decisions made in Washington, their consequences, and how they impact my college community. A vibrant free press allows me to do just that.”

entries.title: Family Sues the City of Alexandria After Son Dies in Police Custody
entries.summary: The lawsuit says police officers “acted with reckless disregard” for the man’s safety.
entries.content:
The parents of a man who died while in Alexandria city police custody last year filed a federal lawsuit against the city and arresting officers Thursday, accusing them of failing to provide proper medical attention to their son.

Allan Tucker II died while in the back of a police car last August after being arrested on suspicion of public intoxication. The lawsuit alleges the two officers who arrested him “acted with reckless disregard” for Tucker’s safety by failing to seek medical care despite evidence he had consumed drugs and was at risk of experiencing medical complications. It also claims the city of Alexandria did not properly train police officers how to respond to detainees who need medical attention.

The federal lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia on what would have been Tucker’s 34th birthday, seeks an unspecified amount in damages.

The city of Alexandria and the Alexandria Police Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

On Aug. 15, 2025, Tucker was knocking on doors throughout his apartment building under the influence of drugs, hallucinating and experiencing extreme stress, the lawsuit says. His family was among those who called the police in an attempt to get Tucker to a hospital.

Once he had been detained, officers denied Tucker’s pleas to be taken to a hospital and instead drove straight to the Alexandria Adult Detention Center, passing a hospital on the way, according to an internal audit of the incident released this summer.

Officers left Tucker handcuffed in the back of an empty police car outside the detention center for 40 minutes during a shift change at the jail and occasionally checked on him. He died lying in the back of the car with his hands cuffed behind his back, the lawsuit says.

Tucker’s intake and medical screening were delayed, according to the audit, which also found that officers violated a department policy that police must give medical care to detainees who request it.

Virginia’s Office of the Chief Medical Examiner ruled Tucker’s death accidental as a result of “cocaine and cocaethylene intoxication.” Cocaethylene is a by-product produced when cocaine and alcohol are used together.

The Office of the Commonwealth’s Attorney previously decided not to pursue criminal charges against the police officers involved, saying they “did not use or attempt to use force likely to cause death or serious bodily injury” at any point while Tucker was in custody. The commonwealth’s attorney only determines whether a crime was committed and does not hold any standing in civil lawsuits like the one filed by Tucker’s family.

An investigation conducted by the Northern Virginia Critical Incident Response Team this year of the Alexandria Police Department and the Alexandria Sheriff’s Office found no criminal wrongdoing during the incident, according to the sheriff’s office. The Critical Incident Response Team is a coalition of law enforcement agencies from across the region.

The Sheriff’s Office, which operates the detention center, also conducted its own internal investigation and found no violation of policy or procedure. The department declined to release the investigation publicly.

entries.title: Northern Virginia Art Teacher Arrested After a Loaded Gun Was Found at Middle School
entries.summary: The discovery of the firearm prompted Manassas Park City officials to close all local schools “out of an abundance of caution.”
entries.content:
A Northern Virginia art teacher was charged with illegally possessing a firearm on school property after a loaded gun was found in a middle school parking lot early Monday, prompting the closure of surrounding schools.

Manassas Park Police Chief Mario Lugo told The Washington Sun in a statement that authorities arrested Veronica Gooch-Ray, an art teacher at Manassas Park High School, after a loaded firearm was found in the parking lot of Manassas Park Middle School, located across the street.

A school transportation employee found the gun between two school division vans during a morning safety check around 6:30 a.m., school officials said in a social media post. Following its discovery, Manassas Park City Schools closed all four of its schools “out of an abundance of caution” to give police time to investigate.

Lugo said the investigation revealed no threat to the schools or community.

Manassas Park City Schools said in an update that the firearm belonged to a staff member and there was no credible threat to the school. The staff member was “placed on leave per applicable school policies,” according to the post.

Manassas Park City Schools did not respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: Ohio’s Biggest Newspaper Breaks Its No-Endorsement Policy to Condemn Ramaswamy
entries.summary: The Cleveland Plain Dealer’s editorial board said Ramaswamy’s controversial ad had “crossed a line that Ohioans should defend, whatever their party.”
entries.content:
Ohio’s largest newspaper backed Democrat Amy Acton for governor and denounced recent actions by her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy on Monday, reversing a previously announced no-endorsement policy for up-ballot candidates.

The editorial board of The Plain Dealer cited in part a campaign ad run by Ramaswamy featuring Acton’s estranged mother, who stood by her stepfather after he was accused of raping Acton when she was a child.

“A candidate who uses childhood sexual abuse as a weapon against the person who endured it has crossed a line that Ohioans should defend, whatever their party,” the Cleveland-based newspaper’s editorial board wrote.

The endorsement reverses course on the publication’s decision, announced a few months ago, to focus on down-ballot contests and stay out of races for governor, U.S. Senate and president.

“We made our endorsement policy to serve our readers,” the paper wrote. “We cannot let it become a reason to remain silent when we believe Ohio faces a choice this consequential.”

The Republican’s campaign pushed back on the endorsement, taking aim at Chris Quinn, who helps lead the newsroom strategy for both The Plain Dealer and cleveland.com.

“Anyone who thought Chris Quinn's paper wouldn't back the liberal in this race is fooling themselves," Evan Machan, Ramaswamy’s press secretary, wrote in a statement. He did not immediately elaborate on that.

Acton wrote Sunday on X that she is “honored” to have the paper’s endorsement.

The paper noted that the “endorsement of Acton rests on more than Ramaswamy’s failure to meet a basic standard of decency,” and touted the Democrat’s previous experience working for the state, meeting with communities throughout Ohio and participating in the publication's 15-part series answering questions from readers — noting that Ramaswamny did not participate.

“He has focused much of his attention on wealthy donors while steadfastly refusing to explain what he would do about many of the issues he would face as governor,” the editorial board wrote.

In the ad in question, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, called her daughter “a liar” and said she has a “serious problem.” The ad did not explicitly mention her late stepfather, with whom Arthur fled the state before his case came to trial, but the message drew immediate backlash from both sides of the political aisle — including from Ohio’s Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, who called on Ramaswamny to take down the ad.

Ramaswamy, as well as President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, have repeatedly stood by the campaign spot.

“Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor,” Trump wrote Thursday on Truth Social.

entries.title: Man Fatally Stabbed with a ‘Makeshift Weapon’ at D.C. Jail
entries.summary: He is the fourth inmate to die while in D.C. Department of Corrections custody this year.
entries.content:
A man was fatally stabbed at the D.C. Jail on Sunday, authorities said, after an assault that involved a makeshift weapon.

D.C. police said homicide detectives responded to a report of a stabbing at the jail late Sunday morning. The victim was pronounced dead at the scene.

A Department of Corrections spokesperson said there was “an assault involving two residents and a makeshift weapon” around 11:06 a.m. on Sunday, and one of the involved individuals was pronounced dead 25 minutes later, after lifesaving measures from staff were not successful.

“The DOC maintains a zero-tolerance policy for violence,” said the spokesperson, who added that in addition to the D.C. police investigation, there will be an internal DOC investigation of the incident.

The DOC did not provide the name of the victim. The department is required to publish notice of resident deaths within three days and at least 24 hours after the decedent’s next of kin have been notified.

The inmate death comes as the Justice Department is investigating D.C.’s Department of Corrections to determine whether the agency has a pattern and practice of violating detainee rights. Among other issues, the inquiry will examine whether the agency has failed to provide safe physical conditions of confinement in the city’s jails. It will also investigate allegations concerning sanitation and nutrition; the DOJ announced the investigation days after a Washington Post story detailed stomach-churning allegations of rats and roaches in food at the jail.

The D.C. jail complex, whose population has steeply risen over the past three years, has also been under scrutiny for a series of deaths in custody. Last year, a report commissioned by the city auditor found that between the summers of 2023 and 2024, people had died in DOC custody at a rate more than three times the national jail average. The most common cause of death during that period was overdoses, according to the report. The report also said that there were at least 580 assaults that involved inmate-on-inmate violence during the yearlong audit period. There were 363 incidents during the yearlong audit period that involved homemade weapons, according to the report, which said that inadequate staffing and outdated jail design could be contributing to the violence.

Sunday’s death was the fourth in D.C. Department of Corrections custody this year, according to public statements from the agency. Marcus Benson, 37, died in May of a fentanyl overdose, according to D.C.’s office of the medical examiner. Another inmate, 70-year-old Thomas Nash, died of cancer in March, according to the medical examiner. Eric Manley, 54, died in January after complications from a seizure disorder due to chronic substance abuse, the medical examiner’s office said.

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: Acton Up
entries.content:
Good afternoon. The Washington Sun has a new newsletter starting Nov. 9: Congressional reporters Igor Bobic and Oriana González are taking you inside the Capitol in The Stakeout. Sign up now. 

Here’s what you need to know. 

THE LATEST

A group of Catholic bishops say they felt “manipulated” and “exploited” after the White House released images of them praying with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office.

  • “I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple,” one bishop wrote.
The Cleveland Plain Dealer reversed its ban on up-ballot political endorsements to back Democrat Amy Acton in the Ohio governor’s race. The newspaper’s editorial board said Republican Vivek Ramaswamy “crossed a line” with his recent ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother.

THE ADMINISTRATION

Trump is quietly pushing for his ally Viktor Orbán to be the next United Nations secretary-general, according to The Wall Street Journal editorial board.

The president confirmed in a Truth Social post — his longest ever — that he is “thinking about” booting reporters from the White House entirely.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed on Monday that Pete Hegseth has delayed shipments of missiles for the country’s air defense systems “for nearly a month.”

  • Hegseth said last week that he had not changed his mind about support for Ukraine, but the U.S. wants “to make sure our guys have the most possible as well.”
Norwegian officials are pushing back against Trump after he referred to the country as a “shithouse” over the weekend — all because he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

THE CAMPAIGN TRAILDemocrats are accusing their Republican counterparts in Texas of withholding data showing how the state’s near-total abortion ban affected maternal mortality numbers until after the midterm elections.

THE COURTS

A federal judge ordered the Justice Department to reinstate Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, to her job as a federal public corruption prosecutor after she was fired by the Trump administration. She’ll also get five months of back pay.

Trump’s White House press ban is facing a new legal challenge — this one filed by a group of citizens who argue that they, as a stand-in for the American public, are the real victims here.

A group of former DOJ prosecutors and human rights lawyers have formed a nonprofit group to assist state and local prosecutors looking into accusations of corruption and law enforcement violence it claims the Trump administration is ignoring. They’re calling it the Rule of Law Project.

COUNTING DOWN THE DAYS

Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Kelly Poe and Jonann Brady. If you liked it, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at newsletters@washsun.com.

entries.title: Judge Orders DOJ to Reinstate Jim Comey’s Daughter, With Back Pay
entries.summary: The opinion rejects the Trump administration’s “new and expansive theory of executive power” to remove executive branch employees.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Monday ordered the Trump administration to reinstate Maurene Comey, a daughter of former FBI director Jim Comey, who was fired from her role as a New York public corruption prosecutor last year.

U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman, who held a hearing about the matter last month, concluded that Comey was “unlawfully terminated” from the Justice Department role after a MAGA blogger identified her relation to Jim Comey — long one of President Donald Trump’s political foes. The judge also ordered the DOJ to give her five months’ back pay.

In his opinion, Furman ruled that the removal “indisputably” violated the Civil Service Reform Act, which limits when and how millions of executive branch employees may be removed from office, including assistant U.S. attorneys.

Furman also ruled against the Trump administration’s more sweeping argument that Article II of the Constitution meant that Congress does not have the authority to regulate the removal of executive branch employees.

That argument “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent” that still holds, the judge wrote, and the Trump administration argument would “unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”

The government has “invented a new and expansive theory of executive power. And they have also utilized that theory to remove other Executive Branch employees who have long held protections from removal,” Furman wrote.

Maurene Comey worked on high-profile prosecutions — like those of rapper Sean “Diddy” Combs and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein — until she was abruptly fired on July 16, 2025. At the time, Trump was seeking to exact revenge on her father.

She sued the government later that summer, describing her termination as discrimination “based on her connection to her father, or her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both.” In her lawsuit, she described how she was fired just hours after the Manhattan U.S. Attorney’s Office had asked her to join a trial team on a major case.

The curt email from DOJ human resources said Comey had been removed “effective immediately” and subsequent paperwork merely cited Article II of the U.S. Constitution — which has become the second Trump administration’s go-to reasoning for justifying mass political firings of career employees.

Comey’s lawsuit described how she met with Jay Clayton — then the Trump-appointed interim head of the office and currently the national intelligence director — who told her: “All I can say is it came from Washington. I can’t tell you anything else.”

In court, the DOJ has since said the decision was made by Trump’s first attorney general, Pam Bondi, who has since been fired. MAGA social media influencer Laura Loomer, who put a target on Comey’s back in May 2025, appeared to take credit for the termination.

It’s unclear whether Comey will actually take her job back, however. She is now a partner on the white-collar defense team at the New York firm Patterson Belknap Webb and Tyler.

Furman dismissed several other claims in Comey’s complaint while declining to rule on one count alleging the DOJ violated her First Amendment rights. The judge said he was inclined to grant the government’s motion to dismiss that count, because it wasn’t clear whether Comey would return to a federal role where officials could remove or discipline her for “reasons that would run afoul of the First Amendment.”

A DOJ spokesperson said the department disagreed with the decision and plans to appeal.

entries.title: D.C.’s VA Medical Center Made an Emergency Equipment Order After Kitchen Concerns
entries.summary: A recent accreditation survey found “insect debris” and “multiple unclean and stained surfaces” in a kitchen.
entries.content:
A recent accreditation survey found insect debris, stained surfaces and unidentified residue in a kitchen at the Washington VA Medical Center, prompting an emergency order of commercial kitchen equipment.

The June 2026 survey found “multiple unclean and stained surfaces, food spilled on the floor, utensils on the floor, food container debris, and insect debris” in the Nutrition and Food Services kitchen, according to a federal contracting request posted by the DCVAMC on Friday.

The survey noted several physical concerns with the area, including “broken equipment handles, cracked floor tiles, and standing water from excess water discharge,” as well as “unidentified residue” on equipment surfaces. It also found the facility’s procedures for food safety and infection control to be deficient.

The survey is run by the Joint Commission — an independent nonprofit that evaluates and accredits health care organizations — and takes place once every three years.

The VA requested the delivery and installation of a custom sink system with a drainboard, a food waste disposer and a pot scrubber. According to the contracting request, continuing to work with the current equipment poses an “ongoing infection control risk.”

“The DC VAMC took immediate action and directed senior leadership to ensure the Joint Commission’s standards are met at this facility, which led to immediate improvements in June,” Quinn Slaven, a spokesperson for the VA, wrote in a statement to The Washington Sun. “The facility implemented new training for staff and a new cleaning schedule over the summer and continues to replace outdated kitchen equipment as needed.”

The DCVAMC has faced other difficulties with staffing and maintenance. In July, The American Prospect reported that the medical center lacked the staff to fix its air-conditioning system and struggled to retain radiologists.

The DCVAMC provides health care services to veterans and their families. The Nutrition and Food Services kitchen supports inpatient meal services, according to the federal contracting request. The DCVAMC serves more than 125,000 veterans in D.C., Maryland and Virginia, and it employs more than 2,000 people at its facilities.

entries.title: The Critical Race in North Carolina No One’s Talking About
entries.summary: A Democratic justice is fending off a challenger to her state Supreme Court seat as Democrats try to keep leverage on the bench.
entries.content:
Democrats and advocacy groups are hoping to fend off a Republican challenger in a North Carolina Supreme Court race on the ballot this fall, as they try to keep leverage on the judicial bench in a key battleground state. 

Democratic Justice Anita Earls is running to keep her seat against Sarah Stevens, who previously held elected office in the North Carolina state House as a Republican.

The current makeup of the court is 5-2 and leans conservative. Even as Earls has vastly outraised her opponent, advocacy groups are shoring up support for her because the court could soon review issues like abortion and gerrymandering.

State supreme court races have gained more attention since the U.S. Supreme Court left abortion access matters to states in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization. In North Carolina, the state Supreme Court’s decisions have been critical on other issues like redistricting and voter ID laws.

“You saw groups on the left for the first time ever spending more money than groups on the right,” Douglas Keith, the deputy director of the Brennan Center for Justice’s Judiciary Program, told The Washington Sun about the post-Dobbs climate. “Now we have judicial elections that sometimes, as happened in Wisconsin in 2025, look like a top 10 U.S. Senate race.”

In Wisconsin’s 2025 race, spending from billionaires and other major donors brought fundraising totals to more than $100 million.

Keith added that donors who used to focus on the partisanship of state legislatures quickly learned that it’s the state supreme court that could have the final say.

The current political climate in North Carolina appears to be favoring Democrats — several key races are leaning far more Democratic than expected. Democratic candidate Roy Cooper appears to be easily leading Republican Michael Whatley in the Senate race, and several House districts have been moving in Democrats’ direction as well.

Earls’ clinching a win in November is crucial to Democrats’ plan of flipping the bench in 2028, when three Republican justices will be up for reelection.

“Since I've been on the court, my record has been one of seeking to enforce the state constitution and all of the rights that it contains that are so important for the people of the state, including things like the right to a sound basic education, the right to vote,” Earls told Spectrum News on Wednesday.

Earls has raised more than $4.4 million as of June 30, with more than $3.5 million in cash on hand as the campaign season closes. Stevens, who has spent little time on the campaign trail and lagged on investing in advertisements, raised more than $336,000 and had more than $257,000 in cash on hand as of June 30.

“I truly don't have an agenda except to respect the integrity of the court and make sure the Constitution and law are followed,” Stevens said in a Spectrum News interview on Wednesday. 

Civil rights groups are making large investments in the race to help tip the bench in favor of Democrats. 

“We just need to change the direction of the courts so that we will be able to both save the rights and freedoms that people have and then also expand upon those where they have been eroded in recent years,” Liz Barber, the director of policy and advocacy at the American Civil Liberties Union of North Carolina, told The Sun.

They don’t want to take any chances, given recent history.

The other Democratic justice, Allison Riggs, spent months after the 2024 election in a legal battle against her Republican opponent, who wanted to discard more than 60,000 ballots he believed were unconstitutionally counted. Riggs won by 734 votes after two recounts.

In many states, funding toward judiciary races has ramped up over the years as both parties battle for control of state benches to make key decisions. The ACLU of North Carolina has announced a $3.5 million campaign in the state Supreme Court race on behalf of Earls, with ads featuring healthcare professionals speaking on the effect of the state’s abortion law.

These types of partisan contests for state supreme court seats are rare. At least eight states, including North Carolina, have partisan elections for state justices. Others have nonpartisan elections, gubernatorial appointments or retention elections that determine some of the most important seats for state law.

entries.title: Is The Cheesecake Factory Really a Restaurant for Regular Americans?
entries.summary: The chain restaurant tends to be located in wealthier communities.
entries.content:
Former President Barack Obama’s mockery of President Donald Trump’s aesthetic choices has Republicans furiously defending the sanctity of The Cheesecake Factory as a restaurant for real Americans.

“Classic Obama snobbery. Cheesecake Factory is a great option for people who can’t afford a private chef at their Martha’s vineyard estate,” Republican strategist Matt Whitlock wrote on X. Conservative activist Laura Loomer called The Cheesecake Factory “a place Americans can afford.”

Scott Jennings, who was on the White House’s short list for press secretary, claimed Obama hadn’t eaten a “dinner that costs less than $250 in years. Has never been in a Cheesecake Factory. Undefeated at condescending to regular folks.” Even Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent got in on the fun and went to eat at the Cheesecake Factory on Monday telling a reporter outside he'd "tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try."

That got us thinking about the iconic restaurant chain and its Egyptian-style columns, painted ceilings and over 250 menu options. Specifically, where are The Cheesecake Factories of America and what are the communities around them like?

Last week, housing blogger (and consultant) Aziz Sunderji released a magnificent newsletter item looking at which chains predominate areas with the highest home prices (Club Pilates, Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s) and the lowest home prices (Family Dollar, Auto Zone, Rent-A-Center).

His chart had one glaring omission: The Cheesecake Factory. Of course, there’s no way Sunderji could have known that in just a few days, we’d all be wondering where The Cheesecake Factory fits into that exact equation.

So we went back to Sunderji’s dataset, did our best to reproduce his work and found that The Cheesecake Factory isn’t quite what Republicans are describing — or at the very least, its faux-marble gates are more likely to be in wealthier areas than working-class ones.

Home values in ZIP codes within 3 miles of a Cheesecake Factory are about 27% higher than comparable areas without an industrial cheesecake outlet, according to The Washington Sun’s analysis of data from Overture Maps, Zillow and the Census Bureau. That puts it in the same class as Lululemon, P.F. Chang’s and The UPS Store.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/qv2eN/1/Much of the Cheesecake Real Estate Premium comes from the fact that these restaurants tend to be located in upscale malls, which we define as those with upscale outlets such as the Apple Store. Though, the Cheesecake Factories outside of malls also still tend to be in more expensive areas.

Where does that leave Obama’s comments? We’re not exactly sure. Regardless, no one, including Obama, meant “any offense to Cheesecake Factory people,” Obama’s senior adviser Eric Schultz wrote on X.

entries.title: Trump Administration Asks Washington State to Set Aside Ballots from 400 Voters
entries.summary: The Justice Department is also seeking a similar move with 20,000 voters in California.
entries.content:
By Gene Johnson

SEATTLE — The Trump administration on Monday asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it suspects registered to vote without U.S. citizenship.

In a letter to the Washington Secretary of State's Office, the Justice Department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by the over 400 people in prior elections. It asked the state to set aside any ballots the people might cast in next month's midterm until state officials can confirm they are legally eligible to vote. The state has more than 5 million registered voters.

“We are asking the state to set aside those ballots until we can confirm they are legal voters,” Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd said in a news conference.

Much of the list was built based on “recent contacts” with suspected noncitizens, Floyd said, because federal officers are now routinely checking to see if the people they interact with are registered to vote. His office wants to compare that list against the state's voter information because that will help determine how many people actually cast ballots, Floyd said.

Without access to those state records, proving someone illegally voted will be a difficult and labor-intensive process, Floyd said.

Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs was reviewing the administration’s demand. His office noted that it had received about 60 subpoenas from the Justice Department since last month seeking information about voters.

“We take our responsibility to protect voter information seriously and will only respond to requests that follow due process,” Hobbs said in an emailed statement. “We see what’s happening in California and don’t want Washingtonians to be harassed.”

The effort is the latest by the administration to identify noncitizen voters, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine public confidence in elections. The request in Washington is similar to a Justice Department attempt to require California to sequester mail ballots from up to 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.

California has challenged that, and during rare Sunday arguments a panel of federal appellate judges questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department’s demand. The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections.

Los Angeles County Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that her staff went through a sample of 200 records from the Trump administration’s list. They found the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, people with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States.

The Justice Department told Washington it anticipates sending the state an additional list of people it suspects are not citizens prior to Election Day. It also noted that some of the people it suspects registered without citizenship may have since become naturalized.

Investigations into prior allegations of noncitizen voters have revealed far fewer instances than the Trump administration has claimed. In Nevada, Trump’s administration alleged there were 1,500 potential noncitizen voters on the rolls but subsequent investigation found zero.

In Maricopa County, which includes Phoenix, the county recorder, who is a Trump supporter, announced that there were 207 possible noncitizens on the county’s rolls. The Republican County Attorney determined there were actually eight.

entries.title: Trump Promises $1 Million Rewards in Exchange for Voter Fraud Arrests and Convictions
entries.summary: “He's really grasping at straws,” one election law expert said, noting Trump has repeatedly questioned U.S. election integrity during his second term.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump promised $1 million rewards in exchange for reports of voter fraud, ratcheting up his administration's focus on rooting out alleged election misconduct ahead of the midterms.

“Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!” Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social.

The White House referred The Washington Sun to Trump’s post when asked specifically about the potential funding source for the rewards and how the administration would authorize any payments.

But Trump’s announcement left election law expert Richard Hasen skeptical.

“I don't take him at his word that he would actually do this,” Hasen, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, told The Sun. He predicted in “six months' time, Trump will try and wiggle out of it and say it was hyperbole.”

Trump has repeatedly claimed that he actually won the 2020 election and has cited widespread voter fraud, despite audits and legal challenges failing to substantiate any evidence of misconduct. The president’s allies have previously floated offering cash rewards in exchange for information about confirmed cases of voter fraud, but Monday’s announcement appears to be the first time Trump has personally championed this kind of program.

The current Republican-led Congress has not yet authorized any sort of funding pool for a voter-fraud reporting rewards initiative, and if Democrats take back either chamber, it’s unlikely that a program would be authorized.

Hasen noted that there are “small, isolated instances of election fraud” during every election cycle, but he believes the announcement “is part of a larger project on the part of Donald Trump to generate distrust of the election system by touting election fraud as some kind of problem.”

Trump has made comments casting doubt on the integrity of U.S. election systems on roughly 70% of his days in office since the start of his second term, The New York Times reported earlier this month.

The Trump administration has also made several recent legal moves to crack down on alleged voter fraud and election procedures across the country.

On Oct. 15, the Justice Department sued California to compel the state to check its voter rolls against a list of 20,000 people the Trump administration suspects to be noncitizen voters. The case is currently being reviewed by the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.

The Justice Department also preemptively sued Alaska last week in an effort to block the certification of the election results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan does not win. Republicans have asserted that Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher who will also appear on the ballot for the state’s U.S. Senate election, is a Democratic plant who’s only running to confuse voters.

“He's really grasping at straws,” Hasen said. “The fact that the DOJ filed what I consider to be the weakest election law complaint I've seen in Alaska at Trump's behest, so he claims, I mean that tells you, I think, all you need to know about how they're scraping the bottom of the barrel.”

Aside from alleged voter fraud, fighting suspected fraud in federal programs has become a key focus for the Trump administration. The Justice Department authorized a pilot program through its National Fraud Enforcement Division earlier this month offering up to $30,000 in exchange for qualifying tips about financial misconduct in certain government programs.

entries.title: Justice Department Charges Comey for a Third Time
entries.summary: “It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse” by the Justice Department, Comey said.
entries.content:
The Justice Department hit former FBI Director James Comey with new criminal charges under the Espionage Act, the latest in a series of actions against the prominent critic of President Donald Trump.

Federal prosecutors unsealed a new two-count criminal filing against Comey on Monday, charging him with illegally transmitting national defense information to The New York Times, in violation of the Espionage Act. The case marks the third federal prosecution brought against Comey during Trump's second term.

Comey acknowledged the charges in a video message posted Monday on Substack.

“It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to,” he said. “Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”

Comey still faces a separate charge in North Carolina, for a social media post that prosecutors say constituted a threat against the president’s life. A previous charge against Comey of making false statements to Congress was dismissed.

Also Monday, a federal judge ruled that the Justice Department unlawfully fired Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, from her job as a federal prosecutor due to her perceived political beliefs.

The president has long held a grievance against Comey over the FBI's initial investigation into whether Trump or his associates conspired with Russia to interfere in the 2016 election. Trump fired Comey as FBI director in 2017, and has frequently called for his criminal prosecution.

The most recent case centers on a New York Times article published in October 2016, which Comey’s defense attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said was thoroughly investigated during the first Trump administration.

“Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone,” he said in a statement sent to The Washington Sun. “Now, ten years after that article was published, the Government filed an ‘Information’ against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit.”

Fitzgerald and Comey’s legal team asked a district court in Washington to dismiss the case earlier this month while it was still under seal. The DOJ responded arguing that the dismissal motion is premature.

This story has been updated with further information.

entries.title: Illinois Man Charged With Mailing White Powder to Four Members of Congress
entries.summary: The suspect said the substance was actually salt but that it “kind of looks like” anthrax.
entries.content:
An Illinois man was charged Monday with mailing letters containing a white substance to four unnamed members of Congress, including a senator who received the message: “HAH enjoy the gift.”

Matthew Unglesbee, 37, put his own name and home address on all four envelopes, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in Illinois. He faces charges of mailing threatening communications and separate charges for false information and disseminating a hoax.

Unglesbee told FBI agents on Sunday that the substance was salt — which he said “kind of looks like” anthrax — sent in an apparent attempt to intimidate lawmakers, according to the filing.

The substance was confirmed to contain no chemical or biological toxins, lab tests revealed.

Three letters contained handwritten notes reading “HA HA,” investigators said. The recipients, three House members and a senator, are not named in the complaint.

Republican and Democratic lawmakers in at least 36 offices nationwide have become the targets of similar suspicious letters in recent months, including Sens. Chuck Schumer, Ted Cruz, Susan Collins, Alex Padilla and Kirsten Gillibrand.

Unglesbee denied involvement in the earlier mailings reported in the news, investigators said.

Court documents say Unglesbee admitted sending his letters after overhearing someone in a restaurant discussing news reports about similar mailings earlier this month. He said the mailings were meant as a joke, but acknowledged that lawmakers would “take it serious” and would have “hazmat come in white suits,” the complaint states, quoting Unglesbee.

The FBI received an anonymous tip on Oct. 16 from someone who said they overheard Unglesbee discussing the fake attack in a conversation at a restaurant.

Agents recovered three of the letters from congressional offices in northern Illinois on Oct. 21 and a fourth on Oct. 23 before the letters were opened.

One staffer noticed that an envelope felt like it contained powder, heard something inside and called 911, which dispatched hazardous materials teams to the office.

There was no attorney listed in court documents for Unglesbee.
